content: Two small sites went live: an Old English dictionary and a batch renamer I wanted to test one question: can one person, with no budget and no ads, get anywhere by taking a very narrow need all the way to the end? Rather than argue about it, I built two things. They sit at opposite ends of the spectrum — one is pure content, one is a pure tool — which makes them a clean control group.
title: Two small sites went live: an Old English dictionary and a batch renamer

content: eldertongue.com — an Old English dictionary The first is eldertongue.com, a dictionary for Old English. The reason is boring and practical. Looking up an Old English word today means landing on a university site that looks like 2003, or digging through PDFs and forum threads. The people who need it are not rare: students reading Beowulf, writers building a fantasy world, anyone curious about where a word came from. So I reorganised the entries as form → part of speech → gloss → example → cognates, and generated close to twenty thousand pages. Technically it is very light: static output on Cloudflare’s edge, fast everywhere, and cheap enough that hosting is not a line item. This one is my experiment in whether content can grow on its own. Half a conclusion: making the content is not the hard part. Getting it found is.
title: Two small sites went live: an Old English dictionary and a batch renamer

content: massrename.com — a batch renamer The second is massrename.com, a tool for renaming many files at once. It came out of my own annoyance. When I clean up scans, TV episodes or photos, the built-in rename tools stop at “add a prefix” or “change the extension”. Anything real — reorder by capture date, regex replace, zero-padded counters — means opening a terminal. People who can write the script do not need a tool. People who cannot write it, cannot write it. The middle is empty. So it is a web app: stack rules, preview every result live, and only run it once the preview is right. One-time purchase, no subscription. This one is my experiment in whether a tool can sell. It launched days ago, so there is nothing meaningful to report yet.
title: Two small sites went live: an Old English dictionary and a batch renamer

content: Two things I am now sure of Building has become almost free. Static site, edge deploy, one domain: both sites together cost less than dinner. The expensive part is not making the thing. It is deciding, before you make it, whether it deserves to exist. Code is not the bottleneck. Distribution is. Both sites forced me to re-rank the tidy technical answers I had collected over the years. Performance, accessibility, structured data — you should still do them, but their ceiling is “does not get in the way”. Being found, and being trusted, is a separate problem with a separate set of rules.
title: Two small sites went live: an Old English dictionary and a batch renamer

content: What is next I will write down what happens with these two — including the calls I got wrong. Not a success story, just: what I thought at the time, and where that turned out to be wrong. If you happen to need either of these, it is there. Questions are welcome in the comments, or find me on X (@craftstead). Both sites are built by me alone. Stack: Astro, Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare Pages.

content: Building and Deploying a Web App on Cloudflare Pages with Next.js, Hono.js, Drizzle and shadcn/ui Lately I’ve been taking advantage of Cloudflare’s free offerings—both Workers and Pages. After tinkering with a few small projects and getting through the initial exploration phase, I’d like to share the process of quickly building a Web App deployed on Cloudflare Pages using these open-source libraries. If you don’t want to read through the process, you can skip straight to the end. I’ve shared the project address; just fork my example project and you can use it right away. Note: Some of the code was generated by AI and then modified afterward.
title: Building and Deploying a Web App on Cloudflare Pages with Next.js, Hono.js, Drizzle and shadcn/ui

content: Preparation Get a Cloudflare account ready. Pages and Workers are both free, but the free tier has some limitations. One important one: the compiled binary bundle cannot exceed 1MB; see: Limits | Cloudflare Workers docs. If your WebApp exceeds 1MB after compilation, you’ll need to pay—5 dollars a month, which isn’t too expensive. It’s much more convenient than setting up a bunch of services on your own vps, and you can also enable Cloudflare CDN. I recommend creating the project directly on github. That way, in the deployment settings you can select the branches corresponding to the preview and production environments, and it will compile automatically as soon as you push—very convenient. Install bun: npm install -g bun I won’t go through the other development-related environments one by one.
title: Building and Deploying a Web App on Cloudflare Pages with Next.js, Hono.js, Drizzle and shadcn/ui

content: Process
title: Building and Deploying a Web App on Cloudflare Pages with Next.js, Hono.js, Drizzle and shadcn/ui

content: Creating the Project Run the command: bun x create-next-app cloudflare-pages-starter. For every prompt that appears, just press Enter—the defaults are fine. cloudflare-pages-starter is the project name and the directory name. cd cloudflare-pages-starter && git remote add origin YOUR_GITHUB_REPO—this step sets the git remote address. Install the required libraries: bun add @auth/core@^0.32.0 @auth/drizzle-adapter@^1.2.0 @hono/auth-js@1.0.8 drizzle-orm@^0.30.10 drizzle-zod hono@^4.4.2 shadcn-ui zod zustand @tanstack/react-query; dev libraries: bun add -d @cloudflare/next-on-pages @cloudflare/workers-types autoprefixer drizzle-kit@0.21.2 postcss tailwindcss wrangler
title: Building and Deploying a Web App on Cloudflare Pages with Next.js, Hono.js, Drizzle and shadcn/ui

content: Initializing the Project You can refer to the official documentation for this part. Create a new wrangler.toml in the project root directory with the following content: name = "cloudflare-pages-starter" compatibility_date = "2024-04-05" pages_build_output_dir = ".vercel/output/static" compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"] Replace name with your own pages project name. Then run: bun wrangler login, and authorize wrangler in the web page that pops up. Delete next.config.js, create a new next.config.mjs, with the following content: import { setupDevPlatform } from "@cloudflare/next-on-pages/next-dev"; /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ const nextConfig = { reactStrictMode: true, images: { domains: ["example.com", "images.unsplash.com"], }, }; // we only need to use the utility during development so we can check NODE_ENV // (note: this check is recommended but completely optional) if (process.env.NODE_ENV === "development") { // `await`ing the call is not necessary but it helps making sure that the setup has succeeded. // If you cannot use top level awaits you could use the following to avoid an unhandled rejection: // `setupDevPlatform().catch(e => console.error(e));` await setupDevPlatform(); } export default nextConfig; Note: If you don’t do this, bun dev won’t be able to connect to the database when starting the local service. Try Running It bun dev Open http://localhost:3000, and you should see the nextj.js page. Common shadcn-ui Components First initialize according to the docs: Installation - shadcn/ui Then install the components—we’ll install them all at once: bunx shadcn-ui add toast avatar badge button card dialog dropdown-menu input skeleton table use-toast These component files are installed under components/ui. Database tsconfig Modify tsconfig.json, changing target to ES2022, as follows: { "compilerOptions": { "target": "ES2022", "lib": ["dom", "dom.iterable", "esnext"], "allowJs": true, "skipLibCheck": true, "strict": true, "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true, "noEmit": true, "esModuleInterop": true, "module": "esnext", "moduleResolution": "node", "resolveJsonModule": true, "isolatedModules": true, "jsx": "preserve", "incremental": true, "plugins": [ { "name": "next" } ], "paths": { "@/*": ["./*"] } }, "include": ["next-env.d.ts", "**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx", ".next/types/**/*.ts"], "exclude": ["node_modules"] } drizzle config File: drizzle.config.ts import { defineConfig } from "drizzle-kit"; export default defineConfig({ schema: "./db/schema.ts", out: "./migrations", dialect: "sqlite", // 'postgresql' | 'mysql' | 'sqlite' verbose: true, driver: "d1", dbCredentials: { wranglerConfigPath: "./wrangler.toml", dbName: "pages-starter-preview", }, }); db Create a new /db/db.ts // app/db/db.ts import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/d1"; import * as schema from "./schema"; export const runtime = "edge"; // 全局函数，接受 context 参数，返回 drizzle 实例 export const getDb = () => { return drizzle((process.env as any).DB, { schema }); }; Note: export const runtime = "edge"; is required for deploying on Cloudflare Pages. With it defined this way, you can use getDb directly anywhere else. schema Create a new db/schema.ts. For the table interfaces, see: authjs import { AdapterAccountType } from "@auth/core/adapters"; import { integer, primaryKey, sqliteTable, text, } from "drizzle-orm/sqlite-core"; export const users = sqliteTable("user", { id: text("id") .primaryKey() .$defaultFn(() => crypto.randomUUID()), name: text("name"), email: text("email").unique(), emailVerified: integer("emailVerified", { mode: "timestamp_ms" }), image: text("image"), }); export const accounts = sqliteTable( "account", { userId: text("userId") .notNull() .references(() => users.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }), type: text("type").$type<AdapterAccountType>().notNull(), provider: text("provider").notNull(), providerAccountId: text("providerAccountId").notNull(), refresh_token: text("refresh_token"), access_token: text("access_token"), expires_at: integer("expires_a

content: How an undefined NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL passed to hc caused a TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace') when calling the honojs client through useQuery.
title: useQuery Error When Using the honojs Client Directly: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')

content: useQuery Error When Using the honojs Client Directly: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading ‘replace’) Recently I developed a project using nextjs, honojs, and drizzle-orm, deployed on cloudflare pages. I chose honojs because it is friendly to edge computing.
title: useQuery Error When Using the honojs Client Directly: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')

content: honojs Query Endpoint Definition export const runtime = 'edge'; type Bindings = { DB: D1Database; }; const app = new Hono<{ Bindings: Bindings }>() .get('/', async (c) => { try { const conditions: Record<string, any> = {}; const results = await getDb().query.someTable.findMany({}); return c.json(results); // return c.json(resultData); } catch (error: Error | any) { console.error(error); return c.json(error); } }); export default app;
title: useQuery Error When Using the honojs Client Directly: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')

content: Route Setup for the hono app const app = new Hono<{ Bindings: Bindings }>().basePath('/api'); const routes = app.route('/sometable', someTable); export const GET = handle(app); export const POST = handle(app); export type AppType = typeof routes;
title: useQuery Error When Using the honojs Client Directly: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')

content: Calling with useQuery export const useGetSomeTable = () => { const query = useQuery({ queryKey: ['someTable'], // Use filters as the query key queryFn: async () => { const response = await client.api.someTable.$get(); console.log('API Response: ', response); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error('Failed to fetch sometable'); } return response.json(); }, throwOnError: true, refetchOnWindowFocus: false, staleTime: 1000 * 60 * 5, }); return query; };
title: useQuery Error When Using the honojs Client Directly: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')

content: The Error When Calling TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace') The problem was here: const response = await client.api.someTable.$get(); I debugged it for two days, asked chatgpt, asked gemini pro, tried many methods, with no result. Just as I was about to give up, I went back and watched the video tutorial: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N_uNKAus0II&t=23162s. I had been following along, and suddenly I noticed something: export const client = hc<AppType>(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL!); I went to check and found that I had defined NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL in wrangler.toml, but I started locally with bun dev, where the .env file didn’t have it. So I added NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL="http://localhost:3000" to .env.
title: useQuery Error When Using the honojs Client Directly: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')

content: Result And that fixed it. Without this variable, hono/client/hc receives an undefined and doesn’t throw an error, which is really strange. Recording this here in the hope that it helps people who run into the same problem.

content: Migrating a Remix Project to Cloudflare Recently I developed a project using remix. I hadn’t done full-stack development before; I’d used reactjs a bit but wasn’t very familiar with it, and I was using Nextjs, which felt very hard to use — mainly because after version 13 switched to the app router, I was somewhat at a loss. Later I discovered remix, which uses filename-based routing directly and is much more convenient, and the loader and action approach is also very intuitive, so I chose remix. Once the project was mostly developed, I thought about how to deploy it. I had originally planned to use Vercel, but one day I saw https://blog.meathill.com/infra/vercel-vs-cloudflare-pages-how-to-choose-to-deploy-your-website.html and still felt cloudflare was impressive (good for free riding). So I prepared to migrate to cloudflare.

content: Node compatibility According to the official , some core nodejs libraries cannot run directly in worker pages. There are two methods; the first is Use runtime APIs directly, which I didn’t get working. I used the second, Add polyfills using Wrangler, adding to wrangler.toml: node_compat = true. Note that the two are not compatible.
title: Migrating a Remix Project to Cloudflare

content: Prisma migration The database was previously PostgresSQL, and now it needs to be migrated to D1 Database. The common Prisma documentation: https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/deployment/edge/deploy-to-cloudflare Assume the database name is my-d1. First generate the sql: pnpm npx wrangler d1 migrations create my-d1 --local This generates a migration directory locally. Then execute: pnpm npx prisma migrate diff \ --from-empty \ --to-schema-datamodel ./prisma/schema.prisma \ --script \ >> migrations/0001_init_.sql The first time you generate a migration file, it will be stored in migrations/0001_init_.sql. Execute the migration file: pnpm npx wrangler d1 migrations apply my-d1 --local At this point the migration is done, but sure enough, something went wrong: near "CONSTRAINT": syntax error at offset 41 [code: 7500] This thing doesn’t say which line of code either; the hinted 41 isn’t it at all. I had to delete line by line and experiment, and finally found it was the error from: ALTER TABLE "tablename" ADD CONSTRAINT I looked it up: https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/reference/migrations/#foreign-key-constraints
title: Migrating a Remix Project to Cloudflare

content: Using bindings When using bindings in cloudflare pages, such as KV and R2, I kept failing to read these bindings. After studying and testing carefully many times, I found some steps: functions/[[path]].ts export const onRequest = createPagesFunctionHandler({ build, mode: process.env.NODE_ENV, getLoadContext: context => ({ env: context.context.cloudflare.env }), }); getLoadContext needs to set env: context.context.cloudflare.env wrangler.toml In the file you need to configure the information for the corresponding binding, and in the dashboard of cloudflare pages, you also need to configure the binding for the corresponding environment (production, preview), with the same name typegen After modifying the bindings in wrangler.toml or the dashboard, you need to run: pnpm run types, that is: wrangler types, which will generate the worker-configuration.d.ts file, and the corresponding settings in wrangler.toml will be updated: interface Env { SOME_KV: KVNamespace; SOME_R2: R2Bucket; } Using on the remix server side: context.env.SOME_KV.put(key, 'some value');

content: A hands-on guide to deploying ComfyUI, installing ComfyUI-Manager, and exploring node-based Stable Diffusion workflows.
title: Playing Around with ComfyUI

content: Playing Around with ComfyUI AIGC was very popular a while back, so I deployed Stable Diffusion’s WebUI locally and played with it for a bit. See: text But the WebUI interface is too complex and has too many elements. It looks very professional, but it’s also somewhat difficult to use. I happened to be busy with work around that time, so after playing with it for a while I set it aside and didn’t continue. Recently I found another particularly handy Stable Diffusion UI called ComfyUI. It looks very comfortable and uses node connections: As you can see, different nodes can be linked according to their inputs and outputs, and each node has its own function. It’s very intuitive. I looked it up, and this type of UI is called: visual workflow
title: Playing Around with ComfyUI

content: Installation Installing ComfyUI is also quite convenient—just follow the official site: https://github.com/comfyanonymous/ComfyUI?tab=readme-ov-file#installing. Note Nvidia cards require installing pytorch first: pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121 Apple Silicon—that is, M1/2/3—can run it too. This is why I got a MacbookPro with 64G of unified memory: see the post. You need to install the nightly version of pytorch, at: https://github.com/comfyanonymous/ComfyUI?tab=readme-ov-file#apple-mac-silicon Then install ComfyUI-Manager too: Just use ComfyUI Manager directly, address: https://github.com/ltdrdata/ComfyUI-Manager. ComfyUI-Manager is a plugin that makes it easy to manage all kinds of open-source add-on nodes. With it, ComfyUI becomes much more fun to play with. Note that it needs to be placed in ComfyUI’s custom_nodes directory, so you have to install ComfyUI first: cd ComfyUI/custom_nodes git clone https://github.com/ltdrdata/ComfyUI-Manager.git
title: Playing Around with ComfyUI

content: python Environment Setup It’s best to use conda for this. After installing conda, create a python environment: conda create -n py310sd python=3.10 pytorch torchvision torchaudio cudatoolkit=11.3 -c pytorch -c nvidia conda activate py310sd
title: Playing Around with ComfyUI

content: Model Configuration Models you already downloaded with WebUI don’t need to be downloaded again—they can be used directly. The method is described in the docs: https://github.com/comfyanonymous/ComfyUI?tab=readme-ov-file#how-do-i-share-models-between-another-ui-and-comfyui. Simply put, edit config.yaml: a111: base_path: path/to/stable-diffusion-webui/ Point it at the WebUI path, and then you can use the models downloaded by WebUI.
title: Playing Around with ComfyUI

content: Usage python main.py --listen 0.0.0.0 Note that --listen 0.0.0.0 lets you access it from other machines too. For example, I start it on my MacbookPro and can also access it from my iPad. Visit: http://yourip:8188, and then—a whole new world opens up!!!

content: More Ways to Play The ComfyUI community is growing very fast, with all kinds of Nodes emerging one after another. Personally I feel it has already surpassed WebUI in popularity. Recently I found another fun one: https://comfyworkflows.com/. It’s a hub for ComfyUI Workflows, where many Workflows can be used directly, and you can also create your own and share them with everyone. With this, you can use other people’s Workflows directly instead of creating your own, and you can also learn how others build their Workflows. For example, I’m currently using this one: https://comfyworkflows.com/workflows/e6c1c436-f878-4cc3-be0a-43ee96864467 After downloading, select Upload in ComfyUI, choose the json file you just downloaded, and then it can be imported. On my side it throws an error: This is where the benefit of ComfyUI-Manager shows. Click ‘Manager’: Select Install Custom Nodes: Then search for and select the nodes you need, for example UltimateSDUpscale; once it shows up in the search results, just install it. I’ve only just started, and work has been busy lately, so I’ll tinker with it gradually when I have time. The AIGC field is developing so fast that it seems to change every day. content: Follow-up on the home server migration: fixing the MacBook Pro's wired Ethernet dropping whenever the lid closes or the screen locks by disabling sleep with pmset.
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro: Follow-up

content: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro: Follow-up
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro: Follow-up

content: Gigabit Network Disconnection Problem The migration is complete and I’ve been using it for a while. The Snail Interstellar’s power consumption is very low (compared with the R720’s 100+ watts); with 3 HDDs and 1 SSD it draws 35 watts, less than 1 kWh a day—very nice. But there’s currently a problem: on the MacbookPro, as soon as I close the lid, lock the screen, or close the remote desktop, the wired network adapter on the Thunderbolt HUB disconnects. At that point I have to log in again; if it’s remote, I have to connect via the MacbookPro’s wireless adapter IP before the wired adapter’s IP becomes usable again. At first I thought it was a problem with the HP G2 Thunderbolt hub, but switching to another USB HUB with a gigabit port gave the same result. I kept testing, and tried an old Macbook with the older Intel architecture—the result was the same.
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro: Follow-up

content: Solution So began a long round of googleing. I found that many people have this problem, but there’s no real solution—they all say to change things in Settings - Energy Saver, and I changed those too: Mainly: When using the power adapter, prevent it from automatically going to sleep Wake for network access I tried every combination of these two options, but it didn’t work. Then some said to check hibernatemode with pmset -g. pmset is the cli tool for viewing power management on Mac. I checked mine—it was 3—and thought it had nothing to do with this. But then I noticed that in the pmset -g output there was a SleepDisabled 0. I looked up this parameter: it means sleep is disabled. Could it be this? With a give-it-a-try attitude, I ran: sudo pmset -a disablesleep 1 After it completed, the pmset -g output was: System-wide power settings: SleepDisabled 1 Currently in use: standby 1 Sleep On Power Button 1 hibernatefile /var/vm/sleepimage powernap 1 networkoversleep 0 disksleep 10 sleep 0 (sleep prevented by screensharingd, powerd) hibernatemode 3 ttyskeepawake 1 displaysleep 1 tcpkeepalive 1 powermode 0 womp 1 The SleepDisabled 1 means the setting succeeded. I tested it, and sure enough—no matter how long, the wired adapter stays usable. It seems Mac doesn’t have a switch like Windows to keep the system from ever sleeping while plugged in. With the M1 architecture, staying on and idle the whole time draws less than 10 watts. Now I can use emby to watch movies anytime with peace of mind…

content: Diagnosing and fixing slow YouTube playback on Apple TV and Chromecast caused by QUIC over UDP through a sing-box TUN bypass router.
title: A Problem Caused by a YouTube App Using QUIC

content: A Problem Caused by a YouTube App Using QUIC
title: A Problem Caused by a YouTube App Using QUIC

content: Problem Description At home, an r2s serves as the bypass router using sing-box in tun mode. I had always used a cn2 gia line, and every night I’d watch videos on youtube on my apple tv before going to sleep, with no problems. This month the server’s traffic ran out, so I switched to hysteria2 on an ordinary line. It was fine all day, but come evening youtube was completely unwatchable. I figured udp packet loss was probably severe in the evening, so I didn’t bother with it. One day I couldn’t take it anymore. In the evening I opened a browser on my laptop and tested the speed at speed.cloudflare.com, and it was indeed normal—downstream over 40M. I figured there’d be no problem watching YouTube with that, so I opened youtube in the laptop browser and found the speed normal, 20K+ Kbps, and even 4k was fine. I hurried back to test on the apple tv, and it was still laggy, with the speed only 200–300 Kbps. I was completely baffled.
title: A Problem Caused by a YouTube App Using QUIC

content: Troubleshooting Process So I tested with various devices and found that, apart from the youtube app on apple tv and chromecast tv, everything else—phone apps and browsers—was completely normal. This was clearly a problem. I also thought it had only appeared recently, so I googled to see whether anyone else had the same issue. I searched separately by the version numbers of the youtube app on apple tv and chromecast tv, but found nothing relevant. So I looked at the sing-box dashboard. When playing at normal speed, the connections looked normal; when playing with youtube tv on the TV, the connection speed just wouldn’t come up and stayed below 100KBps the whole time. It was extremely frustrating. I tried switching the protocol to vmess, and it was actually faster than the current setup, though the speed in the browser and apps still wasn’t great. Just as I was about to give up again, I noticed that on the dashboard the number of closed connections for apple tv kept growing, while the corresponding pc ip was normal. This was clearly a problem—how could apple tv initiate so many connections? Looking more carefully, I found that the connection from apple tv to YouTube had the protocol tun(udp). It’s clearly video going over port 443, so how come it’s udp? I suddenly thought of quic. Could it be going over quic? And quic is based on udp, packet by packet, and when the tun side receives packets it forwards them to hysteria’s port hopping—each (or several) packets change ports and establish new connections, which explains why there were so many “closed” connections. So I googled and found an issue, and tried using this rule: { "protocol": [ "quic" ], "outbound": "block" }, Updated the config, and the result… it didn’t work. Ugh, it was almost 1 a.m. by then, so I decided to call it a day and try again tomorrow. Because I’d had coffee in the afternoon and kept thinking about this, I didn’t sleep well all night. I got up early on the weekend to try again.
title: A Problem Caused by a YouTube App Using QUIC

content: Solution After thinking it over all night, I felt my reasoning was right: it must be using quic, and if I disabled it, the youtube app would switch to tcp. I looked at the dashboard and found that the rule corresponding to the tun(udp) entry wasn’t the block I had set—meaning it hadn’t taken effect. So I kept reading the sing-box docs and switched to a different rule config: { "type": "logical", "mode": "and", "rules": [ { "network": ["udp"] }, { "port": [443] } ], "outbound": "block" } This one is very clear: udp on port 443 gets blocked. It might cause some false positives, but it shouldn’t let YouTube’s quic slip through anymore. Updated the config, applied the settings, and tested: Finally it was normal. If I hadn’t tested it with the browser, I’d have stayed in the dark all along. Now, at last, I can watch videos and sleep with peace of mind…
title: A Problem Caused by a YouTube App Using QUIC

content: How I moved my power-hungry Dell R720 home server to a low-power Snail Interstellar (J1900) plus a MacBook Pro running Proxmox, LXC, and Jellyfin/Emby.
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro

content: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro A few years ago I got into HomeLab and bought a second-hand Dell R720 rack server to use as a home server. But this server’s power consumption was too high—dual cpus idled at nearly 200w. After switching to low-power Xeons and installing only one cpu, it was still 100w+. Over a year the electricity bill added up, and in summer it got very hot. Later I used the ipmi tool and wrote some code in python to adjust the loud fans based on temperature, which made it much more comfortable, but in summer as the room temperature rose the fans still ramped up their speed dramatically. I always wanted to switch to a low-power server. I’d previously bought a Snail Interstellar, which uses a j1900 and has very low power consumption, so I migrated the home server from the Dell R720 to the Snail Interstellar.
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro

content: Attempt After bringing the Dell R720 home, I installed way too many vms and lxcs over time, tinkered with k8s, rancher, and so on. I upgraded the memory to 64G, and could have added more—after all, ddr3 ecc server memory is so cheap—but 64g is plenty and I can’t even use it all; more would just waste power. Currently I’ve kept two lxcs. One runs bt and qt—I use qbittorrent for both, keeping the bt and pt services separate. So far I’ve downloaded nearly 40t of data with qbittorrent: qbittorrent is very stable. I used transmission before and found it unpleasant to use, with mediocre speed. This lxc absolutely has to be migrated. The other lxc also runs ubuntu and hosts the entire media workflow: jellyseerr for searching for movies prowlarr for searching indexers and submitting download tasks sonarr for submitting TV series tasks radarr for submitting movie tasks jellyfin for playing videos This workflow has become very stable and needs to be migrated. Since these don’t use much in the way of resources, leaving them on the R720 wastes too much.
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro

content: Steps Install pve on the Snail Interstellar; this is required. Configure two ubuntu lxcs on the Snail Interstellar; this is required. Use rsync to sync over all the docker-compose files and the mounted config folders that the various docker containers used. On the Snail, use mount -t nfs to mount the media resources and download directories. Change the directories mapped in docker-compose to the mounted directories. Run docker-compose up -d to start all services. And that was it. Why mount via nfs instead of just moving the drives over directly? Because I didn’t know whether the Snail’s j1900 + 4G of memory could handle all these services. I tested first to confirm it could, and would migrate the drives at the end.
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro

content: Problems Found
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro

content: Insufficient Memory Shortly after the Snail Interstellar boots, cpu usage jumps to 100%, but checking with top, it’s a process named kswapd. I googled it—it’s the swap space management process, which means 4g of memory isn’t enough. By default swap is only 512M, so I planned to use swapon and similar commands to create a few GB of swap partition, only to find there wasn’t enough room on the root partition. Because I was just testing at first, I’d connected a 120G ssd to the built-in sata on the Snail to serve as the root partition, but a 120G ssd is too small—the lxc disks alone take up 80G. I haven’t gone out to buy a bigger sata ssd yet, so I’ll make do for now, and later switch directly to a big ssd using clonezilla. First I moved the lxc disks over to the zpool of the mechanical drive array. Being a bit slow doesn’t really matter—these are all background services that don’t need very fast io reads and writes. Then I added 4G of space with swapon, and it’s much better now: The biggest cpu consumer is the baidupan service, which actually wasn’t downloading anything at the time of the screenshot. As you can see, qbittorrent really does use a lot of memory, because there are too many tasks. Hundreds of them—how could it not be a lot.
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro

content: j1900 Decoding Capability The j1900 is nearly 10 years old after all, and many decoders aren’t supported. Compare decoding with the n100: Especially since the videos downloaded now are all 4k HDR, mostly encoded in h.265, HEVC, none of which is supported, so transcoding can’t be done, and many clients using jellyfin can’t play 4k videos. So I came up with an idea: isn’t my MacbookPro at home? The M1Max should be able to decode most of them: Except for AV1, basically everything works, so I installed jellyfin on the MacbookPro. At this point two more problems came up: On the m1 mac, after running for a while jellyfin’s server side would freeze, for unknown reasons. I searched issues on github and others had reported the same problem, but there was no solution. For the MacbookPro I use an HP G2 Thunderbolt hub with a wired network adapter connected. Whenever I close the lid or lock the screen, the wired adapter disconnects. I’d noticed this problem before when using mac’s screen sharing—connecting via the wired adapter’s ip doesn’t work; but if at that point I connect once via the wireless adapter’s ip, the wired adapter’s ip starts working. Solutions Switch to emby; no problems. It should be a sleep issue. Using sudo pmset -g: System-wide power settings: SleepDisabled 0 Currently in use: standby 1 Sleep On Power Button 1 hibernatefile /var/vm/sleepimage powernap 1 networkoversleep 0 disksleep 10 sleep 0 (sleep prevented by EmbyServer, screensharingd) hibernatemode 3 ttyskeepawake 1 displaysleep 3 tcpkeepalive 1 powermode 0 womp 1 I used the command pmset -a disablesleep 1 to disable system sleep, which solved it perfectly. Also, the m1’s idle power consumption is really low—a world of difference from the R720.
title: Migrating My Home Server from a Dell R720 to a Snail Interstellar + MacBook Pro

content: Other Things to Migrate icloud_photo_backup: used to back up icloud photos cron: some scheduled tasks, such as renewing certificates with acme. cups: the printer service. I migrated it directly and configured it, but printing didn’t respond; in the end I restarted the printer and it worked. After everything is done, move the drives over and remount them in /etc/fstab, and that’s it.

content: A walkthrough of prompting ChatGPT step by step to build a shell script that generates Chinese subtitles for video files using ffmpeg, whisper.cpp, and chatgpt-subtitle-translator.
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Background For some obscure movies or videos, it is hard to find Chinese subtitles even though they have a plot, so in these cases you have to add Chinese subtitles manually. But adding Chinese subtitles by hand is extremely time-consuming, especially for long videos. So I wanted to use ChatGPT to help me write a script that can automatically generate Chinese subtitles for video files.
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Approach First, break the process down into a few steps: Use ffmpeg to extract the audio from the video file Use whisper.cpp to convert the audio file into a text file Use chatgpt-subtitle-translator to translate the text file into Chinese subtitles The command for each step is roughly as follows:
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Extracting audio with ffmpeg ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -hide_banner -vn -loglevel error -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le -y output.wav -progress -
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Extracting text with whisper.cpp whisper.cpp can also translate, but only into English. If you then translate that English output into Chinese, the result will be worse, so here it is only used to extract text (English). ./main -m models/ggml-small.bin -l $WHISPER_LANGUAGE -f $AUDIO_FILE_PATH -t 8 -osrt This command converts the audio file at $AUDIO_FILE_PATH into a text file and saves it as an English .srt subtitle. $WHISPER_LANGUAGE specifies the language, which here can be English or another language. -t 8 specifies the number of threads, which you can adjust according to your computer’s performance.
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Translating text with chatgpt-subtitle-translator I originally planned to write a script myself to call the openai API to translate the text, but then I found that someone had already written one called chatgpt-subtitle-translator, which I could use directly. For how to use it, refer to here.
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: The chatgpt Conversation Process First prompt: I described the problem very clearly: what the steps were, what each step did, and my specific requirements. The answer it gave in the first step was: #!/bin/bash # Define variables VIDEO_FILE_PATH=\$1 WHISPER_PATH="/User/gowinder/code/whisper.cpp/main" WHISPER_LANGUAGE="Japanese" WHISPER_MODEL="/User/gowinder/code/whisper.cpp/models/ggml-small.bin" TRANSLATOR_PATH="/User/gowinder/code/chatgpt-subtitle-translator/" TRANSLATOR_TO_LANGUAGE="Chinese" # Extract audio and convert to wav format AUDIO_FILE_PATH="${VIDEO_FILE_PATH%.*}.wav" ffmpeg -i "$VIDEO_FILE_PATH" -hide_banner -vn -loglevel error -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le -y "$AUDIO_FILE_PATH" # Use whisper to generate the srt subtitle file SRT_FILE_PATH="${AUDIO_FILE_PATH%.*}.srt" $WHISPER_PATH -m $WHISPER_MODEL -l $WHISPER_LANGUAGE -f "$AUDIO_FILE_PATH" -t "8" -osr # Use ChatGPT to translate the subtitles TRANSLATED_SRT_FILE_PATH="${AUDIO_FILE_PATH%.*}.out_${TRANSLATOR_TO_LANGUAGE}.srt" cd $TRANSLATOR_PATH cli/translator.mjs --stream --temperature 0 --from "$WHISPER_LANGUAGE" --to "$TRANSLATOR_TO_LANGUAGE" --file "$SRT_FILE_PATH" # Rename the output file FINAL_SRT_FILE_PATH="${AUDIO_FILE_PATH%.*}.chs.srt" mv "$TRANSLATED_SRT_FILE_PATH" "$FINAL_SRT_FILE_PATH" At this point the reply had basically already edited what I needed, but there were still a few problems, such as not checking the return result of each step, so I continued: Second prompt: Need changes: - Check whether each step completes normally, and exit if not - In the `Use ChatGPT to translate the subtitles` step, don't `cd` into the `TRANSLATOR_PATH` directory; set its working directory instead Answer: #!/bin/bash # Define variables VIDEO_FILE_PATH=\$1 WHISPER_PATH="/User/gowinder/code/whisper.cpp/main" WHISPER_LANGUAGE="Japanese" WHISPER_MODEL="/User/gowinder/code/whisper.cpp/models/ggml-small.bin" TRANSLATOR_PATH="/User/gowinder/code/chatgpt-subtitle-translator/" TRANSLATOR_TO_LANGUAGE="Chinese" # Extract audio and convert to wav format AUDIO_FILE_PATH="${VIDEO_FILE_PATH%.*}.wav" ffmpeg -i "$VIDEO_FILE_PATH" -hide_banner -vn -loglevel error -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le -y "$AUDIO_FILE_PATH" if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "Error: Failed to extract audio from video." exit 1 fi # Use whisper to generate the srt subtitle file SRT_FILE_PATH="${AUDIO_FILE_PATH%.*}.srt" $WHISPER_PATH -m $WHISPER_MODEL -l $WHISPER_LANGUAGE -f "$AUDIO_FILE_PATH" -t "8" -osr if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "Error: Failed to generate srt file." exit 1 fi # Use ChatGPT to translate the subtitles TRANSLATED_SRT_FILE_PATH="${AUDIO_FILE_PATH%.*}.out_${TRANSLATOR_TO_LANGUAGE}.srt" pushd $TRANSLATOR_PATH cli/translator.mjs --stream --temperature 0 --from "$WHISPER_LANGUAGE" --to "$TRANSLATOR_TO_LANGUAGE" --file "$SRT_FILE_PATH" popd if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "Error: Failed to translate srt file." exit 1 fi # Rename the output file FINAL_SRT_FILE_PATH="${AUDIO_FILE_PATH%.*}.chs.srt" mv "$TRANSLATED_SRT_FILE_PATH" "$FINAL_SRT_FILE_PATH" if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "Error: Failed to rename srt file." exit 1 fi echo "Subtitle generation completed successfully." I wanted to put some configuration into a .env file, so: Third prompt: Move: WHISPER_PATH="/User/gowinder/code/whisper.cpp/main" WHISPER_LANGUAGE="Japanese" WHISPER_MODEL="/User/gowinder/code/whisper.cpp/models/ggml-small.bin" TRANSLATOR_PATH="/User/gowinder/code/chatgpt-subtitle-translator/" TRANSLATOR_TO_LANGUAGE="Chinese" into the env file Output: #!/bin/bash # Read environment variables source .env # Path of the input video file VIDEO_FILE_PATH=\$1 # Extract audio and convert to wav format AUDIO_FILE_PATH="${VIDEO_FILE_PATH%.*}.wav" ffmpeg -i "$VIDEO_FILE_PATH" -hide_banner -vn -loglevel error -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le -y "$AUDIO_FILE_PATH" if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "Error: Failed to extract audio from video." exit 1 fi # Use whisper to generate the srt subtitle file SRT_FILE_PATH="${AUDIO_FILE_PATH%.*}.srt" $WHISPER_PATH -m $WHISPER_MODEL -l
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Results Finally, here are the results I tested on a macbook m1 max 64g, with a 1:38:50 mp4. In the end: Total time: 622 seconds. Total tokens: 72580 Total cost: 0.145 USD Total number of subtitles: 198 It took about 10 minutes (because my mp4 file is mounted over nfs, so reading and writing the wav went over the network, which alone took 75 seconds; whisper.cpp took 172 seconds, about 3 minutes; the rest of the time was spent calling openai to translate). Actually it is still quite fast. Video screenshot:
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Conclusion In the end this script is very handy. To sum up the above: I personally know linux commands, but I am not very familiar with shell script, and I didn’t want to write one because debugging is inconvenient. Using chatgpt is very convenient. In my personal opinion, gpt-4 is already quite accurate, on the condition that the requirements must be stated clearly, and during the modification process you need to occasionally remind it of the context again, otherwise it will forget.
title: Using ChatGPT to Write a Script for Generating Chinese Subtitles for Video Files

content: Deploy a Local Stable Diffusion Runtime Environment midjourney has been quite popular lately, but it has started charging—10 dollars a month, which is more than I can afford—so I switched to the open-source Stable Diffusion. You can deploy it on Google Colab with one click: https://github.com/camenduru/stable-diffusion-webui-colab. However, the free gpu on Google Colab runs out quickly, and although the paid one is cheap, you still have to use it sparingly. If you have a local gpu with more than 8G of VRAM, you can run it on your own computer to save costs; 6G of VRAM should also work—try lowering the resolution and keywords. This document is based on https://github.com/camenduru/stable-diffusion-webui-colab, and I have added some commonly used models myself. One difference between Stable Diffusion and midjourney is that there are a great many models; choosing a model in the style you want will better generate the effect you want, and it is also more fun to play with. You can pick models on a few commonly used websites: https://huggingface.co/ has many open-source models; just search for stable diffusion. Users there share repositories similar to github repos, and large files can be downloaded directly or via git lfs https://civitai.com/ also has models shared by users, and it is quite intuitive, with sample images, much like instagram—very convenient. Likewise, just search for stable diffusion Some commonly used stable diffusion websites: https://www.reddit.com/r/StableDiffusion/ — the stable diffusion section on reddit; its tutorials are excellent https://stable-diffusion-art.com has many basic tutorials Below I will record the deployment process.

content: A React dev server hit a CORS error talking to a NestJS WebSocket backend; the fix was a webpack dev-server proxy via setupProxy.js.
title: Fixing a Server-Side CORS Issue in React Development Mode

content: Fixing a Server-Side CORS Issue in React Development Mode
title: Fixing a Server-Side CORS Issue in React Development Mode

content: Background Recently I was building a backend proxy service for openai — an account pool for a backend pool that buffers completion requests coming from the front end. The backend was basically done, so I needed a demo front end for testing and demonstration. I used react to build a simple chat front end; most of the code was generated by GPT-4 over several rounds and stitched together. Since I had never written react, it took me a while to pick and stitch the pieces, because CHATGPT also makes mistakes — obvious to anyone who knows, but easy to fall for if you don’t. Once the program ran, because the interface the backend gives the front end is a websocket, it threw on startup: Access to XMLHttpRequest at 'http://localhost:3014/socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=polling&t=OSYSDmI' from origin 'http://localhost:3000' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
title: Fixing a Server-Side CORS Issue in React Development Mode

content: Solution After some research, the CORS problem actually has to be solved on the SERVER side. First, my SERVER side uses Nestjs and the websocket uses WebSocketGateway, defined as follows: @WebSocketGateway({ cors: { origin: '*', }, namespace: 'main', }) export class WSGateway implements OnGatewayInit, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect { ... } websockeet already has CORS added, so it should not be that. The problem is at localhost:3000 — this is the web service the front-end react uses, and the error is from that 3000. After looking it up, in development mode react-scripts uses webpack’s dev server. Per the official docs: Create a new scr/setupProxy.js const { createProxyMiddleware } = require("http-proxy-middleware"); module.exports = function (app) { app.use( "/", createProxyMiddleware({ target: "http://localhost:3014", // Replace with the API server URL // changeOrigin: true, ws: true, logger: console, // pathRewrite: { // "^/api": "", // Remove the '/api' prefix from the request URL // }, }) ); }; Set target to the address of the target server react wants to connect to, and set ws to true.
title: Fixing a Server-Side CORS Issue in React Development Mode

content: Fixing the 'Class Constructor TypeOrmCrudService cannot be invoked without new' error in a NestJS project by raising the TypeScript target from es5 to es2017.
title: Class Constructor TypeOrmCrudService Cannot Be Invoked Without 'New'

content: Class Constructor TypeOrmCrudService Cannot Be Invoked Without ‘New’ Error
title: Class Constructor TypeOrmCrudService Cannot Be Invoked Without 'New'

content: Cause Recently I was developing a chatgpt gateway project using nestjs, with nestjsx-crud to speed up curd development, and I had the following code: @Injectable() export class ChatgptAccountService extends TypeOrmCrudService<ChatGPTAccount> { constructor( @InjectRepository(ChatGPTAccount) private readonly chatgptAccountRepository: Repository<ChatGPTAccount>, ) { super(chatgptAccountRepository); } At runtime it threw the error: Class Constructor TypeOrmCrudService Cannot Be Invoked Without 'New'
title: Class Constructor TypeOrmCrudService Cannot Be Invoked Without 'New'

content: Solution I looked it up online and found one here: For anyone stumbling over this issue: it's probably a tsconfig issue. Try bumping your target from es5 to es6. Let me look at my project’s tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "lib": [ "es5", "es6" ], "target": "es5", "module": "commonjs", "moduleResolution": "node", "outDir": "./build", "emitDecoratorMetadata": true, "experimentalDecorators": true, "sourceMap": true } } And compare it with a project that used to work: "compilerOptions": { "module": "commonjs", "declaration": true, "removeComments": true, "emitDecoratorMetadata": true, "experimentalDecorators": true, "allowSyntheticDefaultImports": true, "target": "es2017", "sourceMap": true, "outDir": "./dist", ... Changing target to es2017 fixed it: { "compilerOptions": { "target": "es2017", "module": "commonjs", "moduleResolution": "node", "outDir": "./build", "emitDecoratorMetadata": true, "experimentalDecorators": true, "sourceMap": true } }

content: Fixing a Pi-hole web UI that refused to start on an Orange Pi Zero because lighttpd could not write to its log directory.
title: Pi-hole Web UI Fails to Start on an Orange Pi Zero

content: Pi-hole Web UI Fails to Start on an Orange Pi Zero
title: Pi-hole Web UI Fails to Start on an Orange Pi Zero

content: Background I recently installed Pihole on an idle Orange Pi Zero to use as the home primary DNS server. The install went smoothly: Armbian -> Pihole. But after it finished, the WebUI would not start — Pihole uses Lighttp.
title: Pi-hole Web UI Fails to Start on an Orange Pi Zero

content: Troubleshooting I checked with: sudo lighttpd -t -f /etc/lighttpd/lighttpd.conf — the result was Syntax OK, no problem. Checking the lighttpd service: sudo systemctl status lighttpd, I found it exited immediately on start with exited=255. Looking further into the logs: sudo tail -f /var/log/lighttpd/error-pihole.log showed the error: 2023-02-26 21:53:03: server.c.1513) server started (lighttpd/1.4.59) 2023-02-26 21:53:03: mod_accesslog.c.612) opening log '/var/log/lighttpd/access.log' failed: Permission denied It said the /var/log/lighttpd/ directory had no permission, so I did the following: sudo chown pihole:pihole /var/log/lighttpd -R sudo chmod 755 /var/log/lighttpd -R Start it again: sudo systemctl start lighttpd And it was fine.
title: Pi-hole Web UI Fails to Start on an Orange Pi Zero

content: How to combine a NestJS WebSocketGateway with a microservice, relaying messages through RabbitMQ.
title: Integrating WebSocketGateway with Microservices in NestJS

content: Integrating WebSocketGateway with Microservices in NestJS
title: Integrating WebSocketGateway with Microservices in NestJS

content: Motivation Using WebsocketGateway as a gateway: after receiving the client’s long-lived connection, forward the message to the microservice through the RabbitMQ message queue for further processing. After the microservice finishes processing, it also sends the result to RabbitMQ; when WebsocketGateway receives the message, it sends it back to the client.
title: Integrating WebSocketGateway with Microservices in NestJS

content: Directory structure src ws-gateway ws-gateway.controller.ts ws-gateway.module.ts ws-gateway.ts gateway.controller.ts gateway.module.ts gateway.service.ts main.ts
title: Integrating WebSocketGateway with Microservices in NestJS

content: Files First, take a look at the WSGateway module WSGateway.ts import { SHARED_SERVICE, SharedService } from '@app/shared'; import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config'; import { ClientProxy, ClientProxyFactory, Ctx, MessagePattern, Payload, RmqContext, Server, } from '@nestjs/microservices'; import { WebSocketGateway, WebSocketServer, SubscribeMessage, MessageBody, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect, OnGatewayInit, ConnectedSocket, } from '@nestjs/websockets'; import { SendMsgDTO } from './dto/send-msg.dto'; import { Socket } from '@nestjs/platform-socket.io'; @Injectable() @WebSocketGateway(3333, { cors: { origin: '*', }, namespace: 'main', }) // implements OnGatewayInit, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect export class WSGateway implements OnGatewayInit, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect { apiClient: ClientProxy; clients: Map<string, Socket>; // 存放客户端 constructor( @Inject(SHARED_SERVICE) private readonly sharedService: SharedService, private readonly configService: ConfigService, ) { console.log('WSGateway constructor: '); const client: ClientProxy = ClientProxyFactory.create( sharedService.getRmqOptions(configService.get('API_QUEUE'), ''), ); this.apiClient = client; this.clients = new Map<string, Socket>(); } @WebSocketServer() server: Server; afterInit(server: any) { console.log('websocket init:'); this.server = server; } handleConnection(socket: Socket) { console.log('WebSocket client connecting, clients', this.clients.size); // 生成 socket_id，存储 socket 对象 const socket_id = Math.random().toString(36).substring(7); socket['socket_id'] = socket_id; // 将socket_id存到客户端socket连接对象中去 this.clients.set(socket_id, socket); } handleDisconnect(socket: Socket) { console.log('WebSocket client disconnected'); // 查找 socket_id，删除 socket 对象 const socket_id = socket['socket_id']; console.log('remove socket:', socket_id); this.clients.delete(socket_id); } // 订阅客户端发来的send消息: socket.emit('send', data) @SubscribeMessage('send') async handleMessage( @ConnectedSocket() client: Socket, @MessageBody() data: SendMsgDTO, ): Promise<number> { console.log('; got [send]: prompt: ', data.prompt); // 数据中加入metadata, socket_id表示此消息属于哪个socket,回传的消息带上metadata就知道发给谁了 const metadata = { socket_id: client['socket_id'], websocket_service: 'ws-gateway', }; data['metadata'] = metadata; this.apiClient.emit({ cmd: 'send' }, data); return 0; } // 此为发送消息给客户端 async emit(socket_id: string, event: any, content: string) { const client = this.clients.get(socket_id); const data = JSON.stringify(content); client.emit('recv', data); } } ws-gateway.controller.ts import { SHARED_SERVICE, SharedService } from '@app/shared'; import { Controller, Inject } from '@nestjs/common'; import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config'; import { Ctx, MessagePattern, Payload, RmqContext, } from '@nestjs/microservices'; import { WSGateway } from './ws-gateway'; @Controller() export class WSGatewayController { constructor( @Inject(SHARED_SERVICE) private readonly sharedService: SharedService, private readonly gateway: WSGateway, ) {} // 订阅微服务事件,从rabbitmq读取 recv事件 @MessagePattern({ cmd: 'recv' }) async recv(@Ctx() context: RmqContext, @Payload() content: string) { console.log('GatewayController got [recv]: ', content); this.sharedService.acknowledgeMessage(context); // 调用 wsgateway发送 return this.gateway.emit(content['metadata']['socket_id'], 'recv', content); } } ws-gateway.module.ts Notes: In providers You need to provide WSGateway so that it can be started in app.module You need to provide SHARED_SERVICE, which is the shared service used for injection; you can leave it out if you don’t have one You need to provide WS_QUEUE_SERVICE, this is critical; without it, WSGateway will only start the Websocket listener and will not start the microservice The above one seems unnecessary; it works fine after removing it, and creating it in app.module is enough import { SharedModule, SharedService, SHARED_SERVICE } from '@app/shared'; im
title: Integrating WebSocketGateway with Microservices in NestJS

content: Summary At this point, the client -> websocket -> rabbitmq -> app service -> rabbitmq -> websocket -> client flow works. I took some detours along the way. NestJS’s documentation doesn’t feel very comprehensive or detailed, and I’m not that familiar with NestJS microservices myself, so it took some time. A few problems took a lot of time to debug: Two WSGateway instances were started, so a connection came in twice; this made the clients I stored inaccurate, and I couldn’t find the corresponding client socket, so I couldn’t reply to messages Figuring out how to integrate WSGateway with the microservice took some time. The main issue is NestJS’s module architecture: you need to import when necessary, and to use a controller from an imported module within the current module you need to add it to providers; if you want other modules to use it, you need to add it to exports.

content: A troubleshooting note on how NVMe power management (APM) caused a severe disk performance drop in Proxmox VE and how to fix it with nvme-cli.
title: Drastic Disk Performance Drop Caused by NVMe Power Management in Proxmox VE

content: Drastic Disk Performance Drop Caused by NVMe Power Management in Proxmox VE A few days ago I deployed a two-node proxmox ve cluster. It worked fine at first, but after a day, when I logged in to the dell r720 host over ssh, I found the shell responding very slowly, and going into the linux container on it was even worse — every time I typed a command, zsh would freeze for quite a while. I thought it was a problem with zsh, so I switched to bash and fish, but they were only slightly better. Opening a local file with vim was also very slow — could the disk be the problem? The system disk on this dell host is a West Digital SN750 1T, which by all accounts shouldn’t be slow, so I ran a test: time dd if=/dev/zero of=tst.out bs=4M count=256 I had no idea until I tested it, and the result gave me a shock: 256+0 records in 256+0 records out 1073741824 bytes (1.1 GB, 1.0 GiB) copied, 42.666 s, 24 MB/s That was abnormally slow. Neither sudo dmesg | grep -i error nor sudo grep -i 'error' /var/log/syslog revealed any problem. It is the system disk and hadn’t been touched since installation. I tried the good old reboot, and found that booting into the system took a very long time. Checking with smarttools showed no bad sectors and no errors at all. I was frustrated. After searching on google and bing for a long time without much to show, one answer mentioned in passing that it might be an apm power management issue and that hdparm should be used to inspect the settings. I looked for a long time, but it had no effect on my disk and just threw errors. After thinking for a while, I realized I had been searching for ssd, so I switched the keyword to nvme and searched again. I found a new tool: nvme-ctl. Someone said to use it to check the nvme power management configuration. I checked its manpage and saw that nvme get-feature is used to inspect power management, but it didn’t say what the --feature-id parameter should be, so I kept looking. On nvme’s official site I found one: feature-id=0x02 refers to power management. I tried running it: sudo nvme get-feature -f 0x02 /dev/nvme0 -H And got the result: get-feature:0x2 (Power Management), Current value:0x000003 Workload Hint (WH): 0 - No Workload Power State (PS): 3 There was a result, but what exactly is 0x03? I remembered that when I checked earlier with smarttools there seemed to be a list of power states, so I tried it, and sure enough there was one: Supported Power States St Op Max Active Idle RL RT WL WT Ent_Lat Ex_Lat 0 + 3.50W 2.90W - 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 + 2.70W 1.80W - 0 0 0 0 0 0 2 + 1.90W 1.50W - 0 0 0 0 0 0 3 - 0.0200W - - 3 3 3 3 3900 11000 4 - 0.0050W - - 4 4 4 4 5000 39000 As you can see, 0x03 is drastically different from the previous ones — it’s basically asleep. I set it to 0x02 to try: sudo nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x02 --value=2 The result was satisfying: 4096+0 records in 4096+0 records out 16777216 bytes (17 MB, 16 MiB) copied, 0.0757074 s, 222 MB/s dd if=/dev/zero of=tst.out bs=4k count=4096 0.00s user 0.03s system 39% cpu 0.080 total 222 MB/s — finally it felt like real read/write speed. I changed it to 0x01: sudo nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x02 --value=0x01 Result: 256+0 records in 256+0 records out 1073741824 bytes (1.1 GB, 1.0 GiB) copied, 2.3109 s, 465 MB/s dd if=/dev/zero of=tst.out bs=4M count=256 0.00s user 1.43s system 57% cpu 2.495 total After struggling with this all evening and about to reinstall the system, I found the answer by talking step by step with new bing’s chat gpt. As capable as chat gpt is, asking the right question matters too — it doesn’t have the human knack for guessing. At last, speed freedom achieved.
title: Drastic Disk Performance Drop Caused by NVMe Power Management in Proxmox VE

content: How I tore down and rebuilt a GlusterFS volume after changing the cluster bind addresses broke replication.
title: Rebuilding a GlusterFS Volume

content: Rebuilding a GlusterFS Volume
title: Rebuilding a GlusterFS Volume

content: Background When I first set up the glusterfs cluster I was in a hurry and used the network addresses of the pve hosts directly. After a few days I noticed that when volume replication ran it was saturating the pve hosts’ own network channel. The dell r720 happened to have four NICs and the e3 host had two, so I took one from each and dedicated it as the gluster bind address. But then, without thinking, I simply changed the ip for gluster1 and gluster2 in the hosts files on both sides — and it didn’t work: it kept using the old addresses, and gluster1 kept reporting gluster as offline. So I decided to delete the volume and reconfigure it.
title: Rebuilding a GlusterFS Volume

content: Process I first asked the new Bing how to delete a volume; it gave me the steps, but I found one of them was in the wrong order. I tried them myself, in the order below: On both sides, stop the volume: sudo gluster vol stop VMS On both sides: sudo umount gluster1:/tank/gfs/s On both sides delete the brick: sudo gluster vol remove-brick VMS replica 1 gluster2:/tank/gfs/s force — note: on gluster2 remove gluster1, and on gluster1 remove gluster2 sudo gluster vol delete VMS start This step errors out saying a peer still exists, because on gluster1 gluster2 always shows as disconnect, so the peer has to be removed Check the peer: sudo gluster peer status, which shows disconnected On both sides remove the peer: sudo gluster peer detach gluster2 sudo gluster peer status again shows no peer remains Delete the volume: sudo gluster volume delete VMS, which reports success
title: Rebuilding a GlusterFS Volume

content: If it errors when re-joining Do this on both nodes: sudo systemctl stop glusterd peer probe: failed: g1 is either already part of another cluster or having volumes configured — you need to, on the g1 host, delete everything under /var/lib/glusterd except the glusterd.info file, then run sudo glusterd peer probe g1 Delete /tank/gfs/s/.glusterfs But it still errored saying /tanks/gfs/s was already part of a volume, so I had no choice but to create a new directory. Important: with the new directory you must mount it first, then copy into the mounted directory — e.g. sudo mount g1:vms, and after it is mounted at /vms, copy into /vms. Otherwise it will not sync. See: stackoverflow
title: Rebuilding a GlusterFS Volume

content: Summary A gluster node’s address cannot be changed casually — you have to set it with commands.
title: Rebuilding a GlusterFS Volume

content: The correct approach (untested) Stop the volume: sudo gluster volume stop VMS sudo umount /vms gluster volume set VMS config.transport tcp gluster volume set VMS config.transport.tcp.bind-address newaddress gluster volume set VMS config.transport.socket.bind-address newaddress gluster volume set VMS config.transport.rdma.bind-address newaddress sudo gluster volume start VMS sudo mount /vms
title: Rebuilding a GlusterFS Volume

title: NestJS: Service Cannot Find Repository Dependency

content: Cause The following code: @Injectable() export class SiteRbacService { constructor( @InjectRepository(RbacEntity) public readonly repository: Repository<RbacEntity>, ) {} create(createRbacDto: CreateRbacDto) { return 'This action adds a new rbac'; } findAll() { return `This action returns all rbac`; } findOne(id: number) { return `This action returns a #${id} rbac`; } update(id: number, updateRbacDto: UpdateRbacDto) { return `This action updates a #${id} rbac`; } remove(id: number) { return `This action removes a #${id} rbac`; } } At runtime it reports: Nest can't resolve dependencies of the SiteRbacService, and the log shows that @InjectRepository(RbacEntity) public readonly repository: Repository<RbacEntity> was not injected.

content: Solution Add the following in site-rbac.module.ts: @Module( { imports: [ TypeOrmModule.forFeature([RbacEntity]), ] } )

content: Step-by-step notes on deploying a two-node Proxmox VE HA cluster with GlusterFS distributed storage, including split-brain handling and quorum tuning.
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE Make sure both pve nodes run the same version Two proxmox ve nodes, enabling high availability with automatic vm and lxc migration
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Edit the hosts file In /etc/hosts on both pve machines, add the following host entries: 192.168.1.229 pve1.local pve1 192.168.1.230 pve2.local pve2 192.168.1.229 gluster1 192.168.1.230 gluster2
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Install glusterfs The following operations are performed on both machines, referred to here as pve1 and pve2 wget -O - https://download.gluster.org/pub/gluster/glusterfs/9/rsa.pub | apt-key add - DEBID=$(grep 'VERSION_ID=' /etc/os-release | cut -d '=' -f 2 | tr -d '"') DEBVER=$(grep 'VERSION=' /etc/os-release | grep -Eo '[a-z]+') DEBARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture) echo deb https://download.gluster.org/pub/gluster/glusterfs/LATEST/Debian/${DEBID}/${DEBARCH}/apt ${DEBVER} main > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gluster.list apt update && apt install -y glusterfs-server Make sure the gluster versions are the same gluster --version If they are the same, upgrade them. One of my machines was 9.2, and even after adding the source it wouldn’t upgrade directly to 10.3, so you need to do this: apt-get list -a glusterfs-server It will list all available versions; then install the corresponding one apt-get install glusterfs-server="10.3-1" On pve1, edit nano /etc/glusterfs/glusterd.vol, and under option transport.socket.listen-port 24007 add: option transport.rdma.bind-address gluster1 option transport.socket.bind-address gluster1 option transport.tcp.bind-address gluster1 On pve2, edit nano /etc/glusterfs/glusterd.vol, and under option transport.socket.listen-port 24007 add: option transport.rdma.bind-address gluster2 option transport.socket.bind-address gluster2 option transport.tcp.bind-address gluster2
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Start the service systemctl enable glusterd.service systemctl start glusterd.service Important: on pve2 you need to run the command to join the cluster gluster peer probe gluster1 It’s OK once it shows: peer probe: success
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Add a volume Here it is created directly on zfs; make sure both pve nodes use the same path to create the volume, which is /tank/gfs here Note: if it’s zfs, don’t use the mount root itself, but use a directory. In the example below, /tank/gfs is a zfs mount, and a subdirectory s is created under it to serve as the volume gluster volume create VMS replica 2 gluster1:/tank/gfs/s gluster2:/tank/gfs/s gluster vol start VMS
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Check the status gluster vol info VMS gluster vol status VMS
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Add the mount Do this on both pve nodes mkdir /vms Edit pve1’s /etc/fstab and add gluster1:VMS /vms glusterfs defaults,_netdev,x-systemd.automount,backupvolfile-server=gluster2 0 0 Edit pve2’s /etc/fstab and add gluster2:VMS /vms glusterfs defaults,_netdev,x-systemd.automount,backupvolfile-server=gluster1 0 0 Reboot both pve nodes to let /mnt mount Mount without rebooting both pve nodes mount /vms
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Solving the split-brain problem With two nodes, gluster can run into a split-brain problem — the two nodes have equal votes and neither will listen to the other. The solution is as follows: gluster vol set vms cluster.heal-timeout 5 gluster volume heal vms enable gluster vol set vms cluster.quorum-reads false gluster vol set vms cluster.quorum-count 1 gluster vol set vms network.ping-timeout 2 gluster volume set vms cluster.favorite-child-policy mtime gluster volume heal vms granular-entry-heal enable gluster volume set vms cluster.data-self-heal-algorithm full
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Setting up the two-node pve cluster Create on the first, join on the second — nothing much to say
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: Create a shared directory In Storage under DataCenter, click Add, fill in /vms for Directory, and check share
title: Notes on Deploying a Two-Node HA Cluster and GlusterFS Distributed File System on Proxmox VE

content: HA setup Edit /etc/pve/corosync.conf Add to quorum so it becomes like this: quorum { provider: corosync_votequorum expected_votes: 1 two_node: 1 } Here, expected_votes indicates the desired number of nodes, and two_node: 1 means there are only two nodes. There is also a wait_for_all: 0, NOTES: enabling two_node: 1 automatically enables wait_for_all. It is still possible to override wait_for_all by explicitly setting it to 0. If more than 2 nodes join the cluster, the two_node option is automatically disabled.

content: Cause This error keeps appearing recently: JsonWebTokenError: secret or public key must be provided, I have already added imports: [JwtService] in the environment variables, And I also added the following in the underlying library shared.module.ts: imports: [ JwtModule.registerAsync({ imports: [ConfigModule], useFactory: (configService: ConfigService) => ({ secret: configService.get<string>('JWT_SECRET') as string, signOptions: { expiresIn: '1d' }, }), inject: [ConfigService], }), ] But JwtService inside AuthGurad still can’t find secret; based on past experience, it should be that AuthModule did not import it correctly.

content: Diagnosing why an injected service is undefined inside a NestJS AuthGuard's canActivate, caused by the guard being registered twice, and how to fix it.
title: NestJS: AuthGuard Cannot Use Inject in Its canActivate Function

content: NestJS: AuthGuard Cannot Use Inject in Its canActivate Function
title: NestJS: AuthGuard Cannot Use Inject in Its canActivate Function

content: Cause Recently I was writing a nestjs project. Its UserGuard is very convenient — it is like, when a route handles a request, the verification code can be handled by AuthGuard. But while writing it, I ran into a problem that took me a very long time to solve, for example the following StaffAuthGuard.ts code: import { ExecutionContext, Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { StaffAuthService } from './staff-auth.service'; import { of } from 'rxjs'; import { AuthGuard } from '@nestjs/passport'; @Injectable() export class StaffJwtAuthGuard extends AuthGuard('jwt') { constructor(private authService: StaffAuthService) { super(authService); this.authService = authService; console.log( '🚀 ~ file: staff-auth.guard.ts:11 ~ StaffJwtAuthGuard ~ constructor ~ authService', authService, ', this.authService: ', this.authService, ); } canActivate(context: ExecutionContext) { if (context.getType() != 'http') { return false; } const authHeader = context.switchToHttp().getRequest() .headers.authorization; if (!authHeader) { return false; } const authHeaderParts = authHeader.split(' '); if (authHeaderParts.length != 2) { return false; } const [, jwt] = authHeaderParts; this.authService .verifyJwt(jwt) .then((res) => { const exp = res.exp; if (!exp) return of(false); const TOKEN_EXP_MS = exp * 1000; const isJwtValid = Date.now() < TOKEN_EXP_MS; // return of(isJwtValid); return isJwtValid; }) .catch((err) => { console.log( '🚀 ~ file: staff-auth.guard.ts:35 ~ StaffJwtAuthGuard ~ canActivate ~ err', err, ); // return of(false); return false; }); return super.canActivate(context); } } When calling the api, when it went through StaffAuthGuard.canActivate, it reported undefined. After adding logs, I found it was this line: this.authService .verifyJwt(jwt) that errored — here this.authService is undefined, yet it compiles fine. So I added logs in the constructor function; this.authService clearly has a value, so why is it gone by the time it is called?
title: NestJS: AuthGuard Cannot Use Inject in Its canActivate Function

content: Solution process I couldn’t figure it out and struggled for several days; I was about to give up. In between I also used ChatGPT to help me solve the problem, and this is what it gave me: It's difficult to determine what could be causing this.authService to be undefined without seeing the entire code. However, here are a few common issues that could be causing the problem: The AuthService has not been imported correctly: Make sure that you have imported the AuthService using the correct import statement and path. The AuthService has not been added to the providers array in the module: If the AuthService is not part of the module's providers array, it won't be available for injection. The AuthService has not been injected into the constructor of the StaffJwtAuthGuard: If you are not injecting the AuthService into the constructor of the StaffJwtAuthGuard, then it won't be available as a property on the class. Here's an example of how to correctly inject the AuthService into the StaffJwtAuthGuard: Following that comparison, that is basically what I did, but it still didn’t solve the problem. A few days later, in between I did something else to change my mood, then came back to solve this, continued to google, and found an issue in nestjs’s official issue list: [# Nest can’t resolve dependencies of the AuthGuard (Guard decorator) #893](Nest can't resolve dependencies of the AuthGuard (Guard decorator) · Issue #893 · nestjs/nest · GitHub) — the same as my problem, also unable to reference the injected service in AuthGuard. One answer caught my attention: [Also ensure that you aren’t providing AuthService twice](Nest can't resolve dependencies of the AuthGuard (Guard decorator) · Issue #893 · nestjs/nest · GitHub), Observing the logs carefully, I found that StaffAuthGuard was initialized twice. The first log had authSerivce with a normal value, the second was undefined. Following this line of thought, I found all the places with StaffAuthGuard, using the // method, shielding them one by one for testing, and found the cause: My StaffJwtAuth is defined in the app, while the controller that needs to use this module is in the shared library it references. According to the official docs (I forgot the exact location), if it is in a library like this, you need to define the guard as global in the app, such as: providers: [ { provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: StaffJwtAuthGuard, }, ], That is how I defined it globally, but at the controller of the api I was calling, I also added @UseGuard(StaffJwtAuthGuard), which caused it to be initialized twice, and the second time the parameter was undefined. After removing @UseGuard on the controller, it worked normally.
title: NestJS: AuthGuard Cannot Use Inject in Its canActivate Function

content: Thoughts Afterwards I did a few tests, also putting StaffAuthModule into the library, shielding the global APP_GUARD code, and adding code in the controller. The result was only one initial constructor call, and the authService inside was undefined. Then I continued to google, and found another one in the official issue: middlewares are loosely coupled from modules, thus it may be better to use them instead. If you prefer to use guards, you need to guarantee an access to the AuthService. You can export this service from the AuthModule, and then import this module wherever you want to use your guard., meaning that in my scenario, in the module that uses StaffAuthGuard.StaffAuthService, I need to ensure it can access StaffAuthService. So I added the import of StaffAuthModule to the imports of the module where the controller is located, and the result was OK. The conclusion is that in the module that uses AuthGuard, because AuthGuard is loosely coupled, you need to ensure all its dependencies are imported in the module that calls it Finally solved. It took several days, and I’m not comfortable unless I solve it; now I’m comfortable, so I can keep tinkering.
title: NestJS: AuthGuard Cannot Use Inject in Its canActivate Function

content: How to resolve mutual references between TypeORM entities in NestJS by mixing a normal import with an import type to avoid circular import and metadata errors.

content: Mutual References Between Entities in NestJS and TypeORM 20230131-152600 When using nestjs with typeorm, entities that reference each other keep throwing errors; following the official docs, I always ended up with an entity metadata not found error.
title: Mutual References Between Entities in NestJS and TypeORM

content: The approach that fails After many attempts, I found it needs to be written like this. Suppose there are two entitys, one UserEntity and one CarEntity, referencing each other. Writing them the following way throws circular import errors.
title: Mutual References Between Entities in NestJS and TypeORM

content: user.entity.ts import { Column, Entity, ManyToMany, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, } from 'typeorm'; import { CarEntity } from './car.entity.ts' @Entity({ name: 'users' }) export class UserEntity() { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number; @Column() name: string; @ManyToMany(() => CarEntity, (car) => car.id) car: CarEntity }
