content: car.entity.ts import { Column, Entity, ManyToMany, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, } from 'typeorm'; import { UserEntity } from './user.entity.ts' @Entity({ name: 'users' }) export class CarEntity() { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number; @Column() name: string; @ManyToMany(() => UserEntity, (user) => user.id) user: UserEntity } This way it reports a circular reference error: circular import errors,
title: Mutual References Between Entities in NestJS and TypeORM

content: Writing everything the official way also fails
title: Mutual References Between Entities in NestJS and TypeORM

content: user.entity.ts import { Column, Entity, ManyToMany, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, } from 'typeorm'; import type { CarEntity } from './car.entity.ts' @Entity({ name: 'users' }) export class UserEntity() { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number; @Column() name: string; @ManyToMany('CarEntity', 'id') car: CarEntity }
title: Mutual References Between Entities in NestJS and TypeORM

content: car.entity.ts import { Column, Entity, ManyToMany, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, } from 'typeorm'; import type { UserEntity } from './user.entity.ts' @Entity({ name: 'users' }) export class CarEntity() { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number; @Column() name: string; @ManyToMany('UserEntity', 'id') user: UserEntity } This way it reports the entity metadata not found error again.
title: Mutual References Between Entities in NestJS and TypeORM

content: The correct approach The correct approach is to use import type in only one file, and keep the normal import in the other. user.entity.ts import { Column, Entity, ManyToMany, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, } from 'typeorm'; import { CarEntity } from './car.entity.ts' @Entity({ name: 'users' }) export class UserEntity() { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number; @Column() name: string; @ManyToMany(() => CarEntity, (car) => car.id) car: CarEntity }
title: Mutual References Between Entities in NestJS and TypeORM

content: car.entity.ts import { Column, Entity, ManyToMany, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, } from 'typeorm'; import type { UserEntity } from './user.entity.ts' @Entity({ name: 'users' }) export class CarEntity() { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number; @Column() name: string; @ManyToMany('UserEntity', 'id') user: UserEntity } This way it’s OK. tag: nestjs, typeorm, entity, metadata not found, circular import errors

content: The left-hand menu of the settings page is edited in chrome/browser/resources/settings/settings_menu/settings_menu.html If you want to add or remove a setting, that is where you change it. To add one, put in a block like this: $i18n{newSettingTitle} Then create a directory chrome/browser/resources/settings/new_setting and put the settings page inside it. Create new_setting_page.html and new_setting_page.js — that is the content. Create new_setting_section.htm and new_setting_section.js — that is the section. Create BUILD.gn # Copyright 2018 The Chromium Authors. All rights reserved. # Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style license that can be # found in the LICENSE file. import("//third_party/closure_compiler/compile_js.gni") js_type_check("closure_compile") { deps = [ ] } js_library("new_setting_page") { deps = [ ":new_setting_section", "..:open_window_proxy", "..:route", "../prefs:prefs_behavior", "../settings_page:settings_animated_pages", "//ui/webui/resources/js:assert", "//ui/webui/resources/js:cr", ] externs_list = [ "$externs_path/passwords_private.js", "$externs_path/settings_private.js", ] } js_library("new_setting_section") { deps = [ ":address_edit_dialog", "//ui/webui/resources/cr_elements/cr_action_menu:cr_action_menu", "//ui/webui/resources/js:assert", "//ui/webui/resources/js:load_time_data", "//ui/webui/resources/js/cr/ui:focus_without_ink", ] externs_list = [ ] } In ../basic_page/basic_page.html add Note that if you copied this straight over from another page, you have to register the name settings-new_setting-page, replacing the middle “new_setting” with your own page name. As for prefs="…", you need to add the corresponding pref name yourself, in chrome/common/pref_names.h / .c. The value path does not take a leading “prefs” — for example, if you add new_setting.some_switcher, then in the html page it becomes: prefs="prefs.new_setting.some_switcher". Then register it in chrome/browser/profiles/profile_impl.cc → ProfileImpl::RegisterProfilePrefs (you can also write a dedicated ProfileImpl to manage it), then add a method in chrome/browser/profile_resetter/profile_resetter.cc to reset the property, or stuff it into another method (which is of course not great). In the header file, modify Resettable to add the enum value for the property page you need, and in ProfileResetter::Reset add the new value together with its corresponding function. In chrome/browser/prefs/chrome_pref_service_factory.cc add the matching entry. Important: In chrome/browser/extensions/api/settings_private/prefs_util.cc, add the corresponding whitelist entry, otherwise opening the settings page throws: ”Prefs not found on element....“ // add by boost 2020-08-13 16:23:59 (*s_whitelist)[::prefs::knew_settingSomeSwitch] = settings_api::PrefType::PREF_TYPE_BOOLEAN; Adding the i18n text Add a new ID in chrome/app/settings_strings.grdp. In chrome/browser/ui/webui/settings/settings_localized_strings_provider.cc, add the variable that maps the id to the webui. In chrome/app/settings_strings.grdp add the new message, for example: some settings Then run src\tools\grit>python from grit.extern import tclib >>> tclib.GenerateMessageId("some settings"); You will get an output id, such as 49303453453534. Use that output to add the matching translation in src\chrome\app\resources\generated_resources_zh-CN.xtb

content: A few gotchas I hit while binding a custom-styled ListBox in Silverlight, from INotifyPropertyChanged to x:Key aliases in the ItemTemplate.
title: Notes on Custom ListBox Control Styles and Data Binding

content: When binding a custom-styled ListBox in Silverlight, there are a few things to watch out for: The properties specified by ItemTemplate can live in a separate resource file. The object you bind to, say an ItemTestData, must inherit from the INotifyPropertyChanged interface, and every bound set property you use must call NotifyPropertyChanged(“property name”); If you want to bind data to the Item object, the custom ItemTemplate style must declare the binding name in its root LayoutRoot. Suppose the root is a Grid and an Item consists of 2 TextBlocks, each bound to Data1 and Data2 of an ItemTestData object. Then under the Grid you first need to declare an alias for ItemTestData: <Grid.Resources> <src:ItemTestData x:Key="itemTestData"/> </Grid.Resources> 注意src是ItemTestData所在的命名空间,x:Key为指定一个别名 然后在TextBlock中就可以指定绑定的属性 <Grid.Resources> <src:ItemTestData x:Key="itemTestData"/> </Grid.Resources> 注意src是ItemTestData所在的命名空间,x:Key为指定一个别名 然后在TextBlock中就可以指定绑定的属性 <TextBlock x:Name="someData" Text="{Binding Data1}"/> 最后,别忘了指定ListBox的ItemsSource到一个ItemTestData的集合上.\\ If you want to add control events inside the Item, one more thing to watch out for: the resource can’t go into the global resource XAML file, because event handling needs the cs file. In the end I found that WPF’s binding really is convenient and simple.
title: Notes on Custom ListBox Control Styles and Data Binding

content: Hard-won notes on rooting an APAD RK2808 Android tablet by repacking its cramfs firmware, then mounting a Windows NFS share on it so movies can be streamed over WiFi.
title: APAD RK2808: Notes on Getting Root, and Mounting an NFS Network Drive

content: See: Getting root on the RK2808 System disk image, plus material on other custom firmware builds A basic tutorial for modifying Rockchip RK28XX Android system firmware images It was a real pain. I did it many times, and I found that tutorials exist but none of them are complete — miss one step and you may end up without root. Preparation: A flashing tool. Download link: flashing tool A ROM. There are lots of versions, some stock, some modified. I used a modified one, hybrid 5.1, downloaded from a foreign forum — hybrid 5.1. Note that this ROM claims to have root enabled, but in fact it does not. You can join the QQ group, the shared files are in there: 83895562 A Linux system. If you don’t have one, just install a virtual machine — VirtualBox is recommended — and throw Ubuntu on it, and you’re good to go. You need the cramfs tools installed, because the goddamn RK2808 uses that filesystem. Google it or BING it for the details; put simply, it is a compressed, read-only image, so you have to modify the firmware before flashing. Unpack update.img and copy it under UBUNTU. Let’s assume you copied it to /home/zzz/rom/ (note: zzz is your login user name) Then run cd /home/zzz/rom mkdir system sudo mount -t cramfs -o loop system.img system tar cvzf system.tgz system sudo umount system rm -r system tar xzvf system.tgz This step unpacks the IMG into a system directory. If you are using the 5.1 firmware, su is already in there and you only need to fix the permissions; if not, go download one: [SUPERUSER from XDA](http://forum.xda-developers.com/showthread.php?t=682828) Then copy the system/bin/su inside it to system/bin/su under the directory you just unpacked, and to system/xbin/su — note you have to copy both. Copy system/app/Superuser.apk to the corresponding directory too, mind the upper and lower case. Then run sudo chown root system/bin/su sudo chown root system/xbin/su sudo chmod 4577 system/bin/su sudo chmod 4577 system/xbin/su sudo chmod 644 system/app/Superuser.apk ``` This step is about the permissions. I failed N times in the past, and the thing I was missing was those first two lines — you absolutely have to give ownership of these files to the root user. OK, once the above is done you can pack SYSTEM.IMG again. ``` mkcramfs system system.img ``` Copy this system.img into the image directory you unpacked earlier, then use the tool to repack it into udpate.img and flash it. Install BetterTerminal, which is just a terminal app. Once it's installed, type su in the terminal and hit enter; you'll get a prompt, choose yes, and if the prompt changes from $ to # that means it worked. If it says Permission denied, it didn't. The following is the work needed for the NFS network drive. If you're not planning to mount NFS, you can skip it. See: [CIFS and NFS modules](http://www.slatedroid.com/nationite-midnite-firmware-development/8087-cifs-nfs-modules-3.html) [Windows NFS configuration](http://ygliang.blog.51cto.com/69909/52898) Install [Windows Services for UNIX Version 3.5](http://www.microsoft.com/downloads/en/details.aspx?FamilyID=896c9688-601b-44f1-81a4-02878ff11778) on the desktop machine you're sharing from. You're all on WINDOWS, right? I only tried XP; never tried WIN7, but it should be much the same. If it's LINUX you can probably just turn it on directly. The main point is that Android 1.5 doesn't support the CJFS format — the kernel doesn't support it — and I can't compile a kernel (I'm learning), otherwise I could just copy an SMB share (that is, a WINDOWS share) into a local directory, and then novels, movies and so on wouldn't have to be copied from the desktop to the tablet — I could reach them any time over the share and WiFi, and just play the movie directly. Sadly CJFS isn't supported, so there was another way, and it took me ages to find it: the NFS format, which I stumbled on by accident on a foreign forum. The 1.5 kernel supports NFS. First download [Windows Services for UNIX Version 3.5](http://www.microsoft.com

content: How a colleague's offhand suggestion turned me into a code-generation convert, and why DBCodeGen saved me from endless copy-paste.
title: The Joy of Code Generation — Marking My First Integrated Code Generator, DBCodeGen

content: It suddenly struck me that an engine which supports rapid development needs, besides a good foundation and convenient templates, a complete set of development tools. That toolset should include automated code generation — the way Visual Studio generates an MFC application for you. It saves us a ton of unnecessary work. Nobody who has used a code generator needs convincing. Back when I was building each system, there was always some repetitive work, and that work was awkward to handle with templates or interface base classes — every time it was copy, paste, then modify, which was a real pain. Then one day a colleague said to me, you can write a program to generate that code. And that’s how, after eating rice for 30 years, I finally learned you can make congee. After that the process wasn’t anything novel: whatever code could be generated automatically, got generated automatically. Define an object’s fields, and out comes the SQL to create the database table, the matching server-side class for reading and storing that data object plus its operation code, the message classes for talking to the client, the client-side message definitions — and of course that wasn’t the end of it. In the future I’d add the client-side handling code and so on. Anything that could be generated automatically, any code that basically never changes, all of it gets generated. After that I found that writing a program no longer meant getting bogged down in all this fiddly work; I freed up more time and energy for the things a system actually deserves some brainpower spent on. Looking back, automatic code generation has been around since the day I started coding — the simplest MAIN function in TC, the APP wizard in VC6, they all generate some code for you to save you keystrokes. I feel pretty dumb now, and pretty unobservant: something that was happening right next to me all along, and I never made use of it. Maybe that’s the difference between the exceptional and the ordinary.
title: The Joy of Code Generation — Marking My First Integrated Code Generator, DBCodeGen

content: A review of Vernor Vinge's Marooned in Realtime — a slow first half, an unputdownable second half, and a mystery about the extinction that never gets explained.
title: Book Review: Marooned in Realtime

content: http://book.douban.com/review/3801851/ “Marooned in Realtime” is obviously the sequel to “The Peace War”. The style is different — Realtime reads a lot like a detective novel — but I don’t think the way it’s told is all that different. Vinge’s novels always spend a huge amount of the early going laying out the setting, the characters, the clues and so on, so with a Vinge novel you have to get at least halfway through before it becomes impossible to put down. “Realtime” and “The Peace War” are both like that, and so was “A Fire Upon the Deep”, which I read before: the beginning was so dull, I spent days on the first half, reading a bit and stopping, and then I finished the second half in one sitting. The real climax is at the back. It makes you not want to put it down. Right to the end the story never explains the cause of the “Great Extinction” — whether humanity partied itself to death, or it was aliens, or, as Della Lu thinks, it was a transcendence. A lot of novels carry that idea, for instance Liu Cixin’s “Supernova Era”, where once humanity is elevated the physical body just disappears. I wonder whether Vinge will write another one about the cause of the “Great Extinction”, and more likely it wouldn’t be about the original extinction but about a second one, suffered by the new society that Della Lu and the others built afterwards, using that to infer the cause of the first. If he really does write it, I’m sure Vinge will surprise me — his novels have basically never let me down. In the end I was going to go buy “A Deepness in the Sky” and “A Fire Upon the Deep”, but there were no new copies left, so I’ll see if I can hunt down second-hand ones. Next month’s big releases are “Three Body” 3, and of course COD7, ha. For now I’d better hurry up and read other things. And pick up a few more sci-fi books. I didn’t buy that Vinge short story collection last time — I’ll make up for it this time.
title: Book Review: Marooned in Realtime

content: Notes on Abstract Factory, Builder and Factory Method, explained by comparing them to an assembly line.
title: Understanding a Few Creational Patterns

content: Abstract Factory is about creating a whole family of products in a unified way. That is, it’s like a template: one concrete factory creates a series of products, and that series probably shares a single style, so different product series get assigned to different factories. The downside is that the product lineup for the series is already known in advance; if you want to add a new product to the series, you have to extend the factory and modify the low-level code. This pattern can be used to control variation — in other words, if I want to make a special modification to one product within an otherwise uniform series, I have to generate a whole new factory. Builder, I personally feel, is very similar to Abstract Factory. The reason it’s called Builder is that the interface it provides doesn’t produce the basic parts (that’s what Abstract Factory does) — after producing the parts it also takes responsibility for assembling and combining them (Abstract Factory doesn’t do the combining). That way the caller doesn’t have to care which parts make up the final product; it just needs to find a Builder that can produce the final product. And by deriving from Builder, you can get parts of different specifications combined in different ways. Put plainly, Builder has one extra assembly step compared with Abstract Factory. If the assembly process and the details of the parts can’t be determined in the low-level code, use Builder; conversely, if the assembly process and the part specifications must be constrained down at the low level, use Abstract Factory. Factory Method is a bit similar to Abstract Factory, but Abstract Factory supplies a whole set of parts while Factory Method supplies a single part. Once a product’s assembly method and part specifications are fixed, you can use Factory Method and let derived classes create the parts they need according to those specifications. I bought the Design Patterns book in 2002. Honestly, I couldn’t understand a word of it back then — I flipped through a few pages, got a headache and put it aside. After doing this work for so long, I dug it out again and found I could understand a bit of it. Take these creational patterns: mapped onto real industrial production, they’re like an assembly line, and the question is under what circumstances you can make that line produce more types of products. The line takes in parts with specifications and puts out a final product. For example, Abstract Factory exists to supply parts to this line, and each concrete factory supplies a whole set of parts — but their specifications match, so they work with this line. If a part with a specification that doesn’t fit turns up, the line simply can’t run. Factory Method is the kind of line where every step and every part specification is fixed. If you want to change the line, you only need to swap parts — you decide which part to swap, as long as it’s within the part’s specification range (that’s overriding the factory method). Builder is a self-sufficient line. The person using it doesn’t need to know how it works or which parts it needs — they only need to know whether the final product it makes is the one they want. That way the line’s provider can redefine the parts and the assembly method.
title: Understanding a Few Creational Patterns

content: A magazine article about Google Wave turns into a rant about Microsoft's lack of innovation and why company culture decides who wins.
title: Thoughts on IT Competition, Inspired by Google Wave

content: Today I took my wife out for DQ, and then while keeping her company over a bowl of Ajisen ramen I drank some iced lemon water. The result was that the moment I got home I made a beeline for the toilet. Of course I didn’t forget to bring a magazine — we have a pile of back issues at home, so I grabbed a copy of CBN Weekly at random, no idea which issue it was. Flipping through it, being an IT guy, IT is naturally what interests me most, so the article about Google Wave was the first thing I read. I’d heard the name before, but only today did I find out what Wave actually is: it turns out to be a thing that combines chat and email. My first thought was that Google always has something new, but on reflection — this stuff has existed at MSN for ages. You chat with your contacts directly, and you can also send them mail. QQ had it later too. So what’s new here? Wave was still in closed beta, though, so we’ll have to wait and actually use it before judging. But that line of thinking led me on to the competition between Microsoft and Google. You could say the cultures of these two companies are completely different, and as far as software — or rather the internet — goes, I reckon it’s these two companies fighting it out. Microsoft has put out a Wave too; Microsoft really has no capacity for innovation. Apart from DOS, everything else seems to be: wait for some small company to innovate, and once it’s about to take off, buy it outright. That’s how Microsoft grew step by step. The method worked back in an era when software companies hadn’t yet formed this big a market, but now, facing a new market like the internet and a powerful rival like Google, that trick is useless. Every move Microsoft makes is aimed at Google — search engines, chat tools, and so on — while Google seems never to have treated Microsoft as a rival at all. Who wins this competition? Sometimes I wonder. Of course I’d like it to be Microsoft, since my own career is tied fairly closely to them, haha! But otherwise I’m not optimistic about Microsoft. Why? Even though Microsoft is currently unbeatable in operating systems (Win7 is just too awesome — once you use it you don’t want to give it up; I once switched back to XP in a fit of temper because PES 2010 was a bit laggy, and after the New Year I missed Win7 again, haha, so I set up a dual boot; I imagine plenty of people are like me), that’s still only that one field. Microsoft lacks the spirit of innovation — just look at Windows Mobile. From CE to 2003 to 6.0 there’s basically no change at all; apart from the home screen, the backend interface has barely changed. I used to be quite bullish on it in the smartphone market, and what happened? Google’s Android came from behind and overtook it in no time. Their interface is simply better looking. Google puts more emphasis on the actual user experience, while Microsoft only talks about doing so. Fortunately, development only comes from competition: Microsoft brought out Windows Phone 7, and it’s sweet. It hasn’t officially launched yet, but the demos alone made me pretty happy. After all, on the Microsoft platform, .NET and C++ are reliable and efficient programming tools, whereas other platforms prefer to use Java. Even so, I still think Microsoft is on the way down. Why do I always think that? Because in the internet space, the fight between the big companies is really a fight between corporate cultures — put more bluntly, a fight for talent. Whichever company’s culture can attract emerging talent better will have the last laugh. Look around the world, or look through history: which country ever became strong for any reason other than its people? Look at Microsoft’s culture — I hear that internally Microsoft won’t even let employees use an iPhone. I don’t think the iPhone is anything special, but there’s no need to ban employees from using one. content: Layering the logging system: a low-level string writer, an XMLNODE proxy, upper-level macros for errors, asserts and exceptions, and an XML log viewer.
title: How the Formatted Log Output Actually Works

content: The low-level function can keep using the old approach, writing strings directly. It gets called by the other log-output functions. Then write a proxy function that takes an XMLNODE parameter. This function accepts calls from all the other upper-level log-writing functions; the upper-level functions unify their log format, put the information into an XMLNODE, and then the proxy calls the low-level function to write the log. As for the upper-level functions, the most common kinds of log output are: plain text output (LOGERROR), assertion ASSERT, and exception CATCH. Make these three into three separate functions or macros. In practice, LOGERROR creates an XMLNODE, writes the log type, time, string and other information into the XMLNODE’s attributes, then calls the proxy function. Then there’s the logging for each feature block. Item-loss logging, for example, needs its own upper-level log function that formats the information into an XMLNODE and hands it to the proxy function to write. Then there’s the server-side log output container, which can filter and display by log type and colour-code them — exception logs can be marked red as a warning, and so on. Finally, a word about the log viewer. The reason for making logs XML in the first place is that it makes them easy to use with a log viewer. Note that every time you add a new log type, besides writing the upper-level function that submits the log, you also have to write the parsing code for it in the log viewer.
title: How the Formatted Log Output Actually Works

content: Why the old log system needed replacing, and a comparison of controllable log levels and formatted output schemes including XML logging.
title: New Logging Functions: Formatted, Level-Controlled Log Output

content: In the past, several of our systems used a fairly casual approach to log output: whatever the problem was, you just printed it. Timeout logs, error logs, ASSERTs, exceptions — all dumped into one file. That makes it inconvenient to read, and it makes it hard to react to urgent events. There was also no way to control the output level. Some output is only needed in the DEBUG build or the first RELEASE build; once the version stabilises, those logs are no longer needed. Log levels should all be controllable. I’ll split this into two parts: Controllable levels: control happens in two places. The first is the compile level, where preprocessor parameters or macros set the highest output level. The other is dynamic control, where a parameter sets the level and only messages below that value get printed. The compile-level value should take priority over the dynamic one, so you can conveniently control how much logging gets shown. Formatted output: the old logs were sloppy and couldn’t be formatted. I did once try formatted output before — in the new system, for example, the “valuables flow” log. That kind of log separates fields with spaces, so a tool can read it easily for filtering and querying, and it’s fairly fast too. The downside is that the format is rigid and very strict, so it only works for systems that share a common structure. Another formatted approach is XML: different kinds of logs can be distinguished by different markers, each can carry its own attributes, and tools can inspect them conveniently. The biggest problem is file size — it multiplies the number of bytes written to the log. A final approach is to split logs across different files, but that produces a pile of files and makes it awkward for tools to search through them. Personally I lean towards XML. Yes, the log gets bloated, but it’s easy to manage and a tool can query it very easily. A lot of the low-level logging doesn’t use that approach though, so I need to estimate how big a change this would be. The other problem I can’t solve right now is “duplicate logs”. If there’s an error that gets recorded on every heartbeat, the log fills up with them and wastes a lot of space — logs routinely run to hundreds of megabytes. I still haven’t found a way around that.
title: New Logging Functions: Formatted, Level-Controlled Log Output

content: How a time sync service pushing the clock backwards turned a DWORD time difference into a huge positive number, and how to guard against it.
title: The Trouble Caused by the Server's Automatic Time Sync Service

content: Soldiers Sortie had an outage once, and the cause was the sync service pulling the time backwards. That meant the current time could end up earlier than the timestamp of an event already recorded in memory, so subtracting one from the other produced a negative number — and since we were using DWORD, it became an enormous value and corrupted the data. The fix: first, it’s best to turn off the time sync service on the server; then check the DWORD difference and skip the operation if it’s negative. I think DWORD has to be used with care — I’ve run into trouble on this more than once!
title: The Trouble Caused by the Server's Automatic Time Sync Service

content: Using a functor instead of std::less so a priority_queue of pointers compares a member of the pointed-to object rather than the pointer values.
title: When the Elements of a Priority Queue Are Pointers

content: Using a priority queue whose elements are pointers, like this: typedef priority_queue<TimeEvent*, deque <TimeEvent*>, less<deque<TimeEvent*>::value_type> TIME_EVENT_QUEUE; Compared this way, the result is a comparison of pointer values. If I want to compare some member of TimeEvent, that doesn’t work. After some Googling, there’s an approach: replace less with a functor struct: struct TimeEventLessComp { bool operator () (TimeEvent*& a, TimeEvent*& b) const { return a->dwTick > b->dwTick; }; }; Then change the declaration to: typedef priority_queue<TimeEvent*, deque <TimeEvent*>, TimeEventLessComp> TIME_EVENT_QUEUE;
title: When the Elements of a Priority Queue Are Pointers

content: A quick benchmark showing a priority_queue beats sorting a list for a timer service with 500,000 events.
title: Test Results for the Time Service

content: After a simple test: generate 500,000 timers, then insert the pointers into a list and into a priority_queue respectively, with the priority_queue using a vector container (it can’t use list). First I used list’s own sort function: 516ms, and I ran it several times, always above 500ms and below 550ms. For the priority_queue, on top of the existing 500,000 I did 100,000 insertions, 31ms in total, 0.00031ms per event on average. The output looks like this: list sort time:516 ms priority_queue push 100000 event use 31 ms time, average 0.000310 ms per event sorted list sort time:516 ms sorted list trace 0 sorted list trace 1 …. priority_queue trace 0 priority_queue trace 1 …. So the test shows the priority queue is clearly faster than sorting the LIST myself — a great fit for what I need!
title: Test Results for the Time Service

content: Sketching a game server time service built on a timer queue, plus two open questions about timer resolution and tick overflow.
title: How to Implement a Time Service

content: Use a singly or doubly linked list, or a priority queue (priority_queue). Each element in the queue is a timer object. A timer object holds the time difference measured from a standard point in time (when the program started running) — the later a timer is supposed to fire, the larger this value — along with the trigger event type. If you only use a linked list, you have to re-sort after every insertion. With a priority queue the insertion position is handled automatically, so I figure the priority queue should work better, though I still need to test it. On every heartbeat (the server thread loop), the time service’s OnTicker function is called. It checks the time value of the first timer in the queue, and if the current time difference has reached or passed it, the timer is popped out and its trigger event is called. Right now there are two questions still unanswered: How precise should the time difference be? The best case would be microsecond precision, but then the queue in the time service could grow to hundreds of thousands of entries — how much would that hurt insertion? Needs actual testing. How should the time difference be set? The TICK I’m using now is a DWORD, 32 bits, over 4.2 billion milliseconds, which is 49.71 days in days. If I just store the system TICK plus the time needed until the trigger event, it will very likely overflow. If instead I take the program start time as zero and call the system TICK at that moment SYSTEM_TICK, then use that as the reference, the time value EVENT_TICK of a newly added event is: EVENT_TICK = NOW_TICK (current system TICK) - SYSTEM_TICK + NEED_TIME (the needed time). In other words there’s a conversion step when storing. That way I can store triggers up to 49 days from program start. Haven’t quite worked this out yet.
title: How to Implement a Time Service

content: Adding a database-operation counter to hunt down excessive queries at login, and discovering that the WEBSERVICE-based auto-activation was costing 125ms per call.
title: Load Testing Notes 2

content: Yesterday I found that at login the task initialisation was hitting the database far too often. Today, to find the other hot spots for database operations, I added a database-operation counter variable: if the operations get too frequent during login or while running certain calculations, I dump the database operation log and track down the cause. I changed the way tasks are initialised, but now the problem is that auto-activation uses WEBSERVICE, and it’s far too slow. Not counting the database query time, just calling the web service function alone costs 125MS. Way too slow — I definitely need to build a middle server.
title: Load Testing Notes 2

content: First round of closed-beta stress testing: a one-second login that will not scale, 900-odd player tasks each hitting the database, and a log writer that hangs the server.
title: Stress Testing Notes 1

content: Closed beta is almost here, so we’ve started stress testing. 1000 connections was fine, but the problems showed up after login: handling a single login takes one second, so you can imagine how long 1000 of them would take. That obviously won’t do. So I added some test statements to find out who was dragging things out. In the end it turned out to be the player task initialisation at login — there are over 900 tasks, each with sub-tasks, and every sub-task does a SELECT against the database whether or not there’s a record. No wonder. Tomorrow I’ll get someone to fix it: completed tasks and tasks that haven’t started yet don’t need to be read at all. That should speed things up a lot. Then I found another problem with log writing. In the function called on every TICK, if a CHECK-style log fires an error, it keeps writing and the server stops responding. Apart from turning off logging to disk, there’s almost nothing else you can do. When the UI thread displays things, each time it pulls a log message it now checks whether that would exceed the time available for this TICK; if it would, the unprocessed TICKs get handled next time, so the UI doesn’t freeze.
title: Stress Testing Notes 1

content: Chasing down WSAENOBUFS error 10055 on a load-test client that opened a thousand connections, and finding that only more threads actually helped.
title: Windows Socket Notes

content: Error 10055: as soon as the load-test client opened 1000 connections, it threw error 10055. I looked it up and found it meant a lack of resources. Thinking about it afterwards, it must have been connecting too fast — the server couldn’t keep up, so the client’s buffer filled up. The fix is to add more threads, or pause a little between each connection. Later I found that pausing between connections didn’t help at all; only adding threads did.
title: Windows Socket Notes

content: A late-night office viewing of The Family Man leads to brooding about whether the price of the good life is isolation.
title: Nicolas Cage in The Family Man

content: When I watched this film I was on a long business trip away from home. I wouldn’t say my career was really on the up, but at least I hadn’t yet thought about going back to Wuhan. I saw it on an ordinary weekday, after work, with nowhere to go, alone in the office. It runs less than two hours, and yet it felt as though I had lived through a good long stretch of time alongside the protagonist, Jack. Over that stretch Jack goes through an illusory experience, transforming from a rich bachelor who has everything and therefore nothing into a homebody who puts family above all. I have to say the plot of this film is utterly absurd and simply could not happen. And yet I believe that if Jack had made the choice, at the very start of the film, to stay with his girlfriend, then maybe his life really would have unfolded along that invented storyline. A person’s choices decide his fate. Once Jack gives up his girlfriend he rises steadily, until he has his own patch of territory in a high-rise Wall Street office, different women throw themselves at him every day, and the closet in his spacious bedroom holds countless designer outfits for him to pick from, as if he ran a clothing shop himself. There’s a long take in the film where Jack, humming a Pavarotti tune while he showers, opens his ultra-luxurious closet, casually picks out some exquisite garment, and then stands in front of the mirror. My god. I remember thinking at that moment: maybe this is the life I want. No — this is the life every Chinese person wants. If the film had been nothing but the life of a rich bachelor, I’d probably have forgotten the story the next day, and it would have lowered Cage in my estimation as well. In fact Cage didn’t let me down, and the good part comes later: on Christmas Eve, Cage is alone in a small supermarket (a rich bachelor doesn’t have much family, after all) when he runs into a black man who is holding up the place at gunpoint because he wrongly believes Jack forged his lottery ticket. To avoid trouble, Jack settles the matter with his own money. In return the man gives him a bell and says a whole lot of things that leave Jack completely baffled. Jack goes home, puts the bell on the bed, and falls asleep. At this point the story opens a new thread, and one I absolutely did not see coming: the next morning he is woken up by his own daughter and the dog. Strange — wasn’t he a rich bachelor? The film now drops Jack into the life he would have led had he never left his girlfriend, a life of settling down and living happily ever after. If a man’s whole life turns upside down within a single day, he’d surely go mad. And if he goes from being a rich bachelor who lacks nothing to a family man who is harassed by the kids every day and frets about money every waking hour, what then? Jack falls apart. Everything he had no longer belongs to him — his apartment, his sports car, his status, his women, all of it gone, replaced by children who make a racket every day, a wife who nags at him nonstop, and a boring job selling car tyres. So Jack starts looking for a way out. He finds the black man, who has taken over Jack’s position, and who tells him that when the bell rings again Jack will return to his former life. I don’t feel like telling the rest of the story — go and watch the film yourselves. The ending is a lot of fun anyway. After finishing it I couldn’t calm down for a long time. There was too much to think about: what kind of life do I actually want, what am I really chasing? A high-quality material life is what everyone wants, but if the price you pay for it is spiritual isolation and poverty, how do you choose? Maybe most people are like Jack after he becomes an ordinary man — tedious, bored, helpless, forever fantasising about making it big, and nobody ever stops to ask what the cost of that kind of life might be. content: A short excerpt from Advanced Animation with DirectX on interpolating bone transformation matrices between key frames.
title: Excerpt: Coordinate Interpolation in Skeletal Animation

content: Excerpted from: Advanced.Animation.with.DirectX Here’s where using key frames comes in handy. Suppose you want to calculate the orientation of the bones at a specific time say, at 648 milliseconds. That time just so happens to fall between the second and third keys (148 milliseconds past the second key). Now, assume that the two transformation matrices represent the orientations of each bone in the animation. D3DXMATRIX matKey1, matKey2; By taking each key and interpolating the values between them, you can come up with a transformation to use at any time between the keys. In this example, at 648 milliseconds in the animation, you can interpolate the transformations as follows: // Get the difference in the matrices D3DXMATRIX matTransformation = matKey2 − MatKey1; // 请坐标位移 // Get keys' times float Key1Time = 500.0f; float Key2Time = 1200.0f; // Get the time difference of the keys float TimeDiff = Key2Time − Key1Time; // 算出时间差 // Get the scalar from animation time and time difference float Scalar = (648.0f − Key1Time) / TimeDiff; // 当前帧在两关键帧中间的比值 // Calculate the interpolated transformation matrix matTransformation *= Scalar; // 算出当前帧的相对变换矩阵 matTransformation += matKey1; // 算出最终的当前帧的变换矩阵
title: Excerpt: Coordinate Interpolation in Skeletal Animation

content: A commute ruined by a 52-day road closure in Wuhan, and some grumbling about how the traffic authorities handle things.
title: Wuhan's Traffic Has Become a Bottleneck for the City's Growth!

content: Yesterday a colleague gave me the bad news: Changqing Road is being closed — closed for 52 days — and the 800,000 people over there will all be funnelling through Gusaoshu Road, which I pass every single day. God. It already took me nearly two hours to get from Hankou to Wuchang for work every day, and now this. Ugh. Sure enough, I didn’t get home until after eight last night. What a jam. I really don’t know how a developing country like China has so many cars! Today I read the news online. The reporter said: 3 kilometres took 40 minutes. Original article: http://hb.qq.com/a/20080806/000042.htm And then a traffic cop actually says “the traffic volume on these roads was already close to saturation on a normal day; yesterday’s congestion was still within an acceptable range.” Ugh. Speechless. Chinese people are numb to this too! “According to reports, to support these traffic control measures the traffic management department deployed more than 200 police officers to direct traffic, and set up over 100 diversion posts and 220 direction signs along the route, effectively relieving pressure in the controlled area.” So the police were there — I just didn’t see 200 of them. I’d be surprised if there were 20! “The reporter learned on site that quite a few drivers still didn’t know about the closed construction here. Some saw that buses and taxis could get through, so they ‘played dumb’ and drove in. One traffic officer explained that to avoid blocking the intersection by stopping cars there, they did not force a stop while the side lanes were still flowing fairly normally — but that doesn’t mean there are no electronic police cameras inside the restricted zone. Vehicles that barge in will face penalties.” Let’s not even talk about their ability to solve traffic problems. Fining people and collecting money — first class, that. “The Wuhan Traffic Management Bureau and the contractor, China Railway 11th Bureau Group, explained that the full-closure plan was decided after weighing the options repeatedly: the construction side drew up three plans, requiring half-closure, full-closure and half-closure respectively, with construction periods of 104 days, 52 days and 192 days. With a half-closure, the already heavy traffic would all be squeezed onto half the road surface, and conditions would inevitably get worse; on top of that the construction period would be longer, so it was not the better choice. The full-closure plan needs the shortest construction period. Bearing in mind that ‘a long pain is worse than a short one’, they decided on the second plan.” Poor drivers. We pay every tax under the sun, the bridge is only crossable 365/2 days a year, and now the roads aren’t usable either — all we can do is squeeze onto the rest. This morning I left 20 minutes early for work, thinking I’d arrive early. Jams everywhere: Shiqiao, Tangjiadun, Beihu, Hangkong Road, the Yangtze River Bridge, Yuemachang, Fujiapo… The subway — when on earth will it be finished?
title: Wuhan's Traffic Has Become a Bottleneck for the City's Growth!

content: Vertical sync doesn't work in D3D8 windowed mode, so the demo tore — plus the DX9 rewrite needed to copy a render target back to system memory.
title: D3D8 Windowed Mode Vsync! Fighting Tearing!

content: Today the boss said the DEMO felt a bit choppy. One look and it turned out to be a vertical sync problem! So I added the vsync attribute to HGE’s parameters — no dice. A bit of reading and I found that D3D8 can only do vertical sync in fullscreen mode. Almighty Microsoft, are you doing this to us on purpose? I dug up some references. This lack of sync is called Image Tearing. Roughly: the data the graphics card sends to the monitor goes row by row, not a whole screen at a time, so when the card has sent part of a screen and you write data into video memory at that moment, the image ends up misaligned! Original article: www.virtualdub.org/blog/pivot/entry.php As for a fix, I searched all afternoon and found nothing that works with D3D8. I even tried using GetRasterStatus to check whether the current frame had finished being sent — that didn’t work either! Looks like the only option is to move to D3D9! Eventually I switched to DX9 and it seemed fine. Then in the afternoon, after a full day of work, I opened the program and the image was misaligned again. Later I worked out the likely cause: in windowed mode DX isn’t exclusive, so the GID can grab resources. If you have a lot of programs open and a weak graphics card (mine is Intel integrated graphics), it can stutter. That’s only a guess though — I haven’t pinned down the actual cause yet! After switching to DX9 the TEARING problem was solved, but a new problem came with it. DX9 made a lot of changes compared with DX8, and the old program had a mechanism built on DX8: render a series of alpha textures into a render surface, then render that surface’s texture into the main scene. Because HGE uses DX8, D3DXCreateTexture created a texture of type D3DUSAGE_RENDERTARGET in D3DPOOL_DEFAULT (video memory; the DX8 DOC says: This is usually video memory, including both local video memory and AGP memory), so you can’t lock it directly to get an address and copy. You first had to call CreateImageSurface to create an image surface in D3DPOOL_SYSTEMMEM (system memory, Consumes system RAM but does not reduce pageable RAM.), call CopyRects to copy the surface from video memory into the image surface in memory, then LockRect the in-memory image surface and stream its data into the new texture! That’s the DX8 way. In DX9 it’s all different: first, CopyRects is gone, CreateImageSurface is gone. After a lot of debugging and experimenting, I ended up using CreateOffscreenPlainSurface in D3DPOOL_SYSTEMMEM to replace CreateImageSurface, and GetRenderTargetData to copy the surface from video memory into the in-memory surface! Along the way I found the DX9 functions that correspond to DX8’s CopyRects: Function Source surface pool Destination surface pool GetRenderTargetData POOL_DEFAULT D3DPOOL_SYSTEMMEM UpdateSurface D3DPOOL_SYSTEMMEM D3DPOOL_DEFAULT One last thing: Microsoft’s DX interfaces keep changing, which is really annoying — maybe I’m just not used to it! Even different versions of DX9 keep changing!
title: D3D8 Windowed Mode Vsync! Fighting Tearing!
